Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
MSL-7 is a potent, synthetic small‐molecule activator of transcription factor EB (TFEB) that was discovered through high‐content screening methodologies and is commercially available (Cayman Chemical catalog #14818). This candidate belongs to a novel class of autophagy enhancers that exploit the calcium–calcineurin signaling pathway rather than the classical mTOR inhibition mechanism to induce nuclear translocation of TFEB (Lim et al., 2018). Unlike many mTOR inhibitors that produce a broader range of kinase and metabolic inhibition with considerable off‐target effects, MSL-7 is designed to selectively elevate cytosolic calcium in target cells, leading to the activation of the phosphatase calcineurin and subsequent dephosphorylation of TFEB (Lim et al., 2018). Subsequently, dephosphorylated TFEB translocates to the nucleus, where it binds to coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) motifs and activates the transcription of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Chen et al., 2021). As a member of the small-molecule TFEB activators, MSL-7 represents a targeted therapeutic approach that has been primarily studied for metabolic disorders and neurodegenerative conditions and now is being considered for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) due to the critical role of lysosomal dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) pathology (Lim et al., 2018; Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of molecules that modulate TFEB activity spans multiple disease areas, including metabolic syndrome, neurodegeneration, and lysosomal storage disorders. MSL-7 itself has been evaluated in preclinical models for metabolic syndrome, showing promising metabolic improvements via its activation of the calcium–calcineurin–TFEB axis (Lim et al., 2018). In these studies, MSL-7 reversed metabolic changes through enhanced autophagic flux and improved lysosomal clearance, setting a precedent for its application in diseases where accumulation of toxic aggregates is central to pathology (Lim et al., 2018). Although MSL-7 has not been directly used for the treatment of dry AMD in clinical studies, considerable evidence from biochemical and cellular studies supports the concept that activation of TFEB can ameliorate age-dependent RPE dysfunction by promoting the clearance of lipofuscin and other toxic aggregates (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025). Prior studies of other TFEB activators—such as trehalose, which has been shown to enhance autophagic clearance in RPE cells—provide a robust rationale for the application of MSL-7 in retinal degenerative models (Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Moreover, the involvement of the autophagy–lysosomal network in maintaining retinal health and its impairment in AMD have been well documented, suggesting that strategies to enhance autophagic clearance via TFEB activation are both mechanistically sound and therapeutically appealing (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism of MSL-7 centers on its ability to modulate intracellular calcium dynamics, which is critical for the activation of the phosphatase calcineurin. Under physiological conditions, TFEB remains phosphorylated and sequestered in the cytoplasm by the action of mTORC1 and possibly other kinases; however, when MSL-7 is applied, it elevates cytosolic calcium levels specifically in RPE cells, thereby leading to the activation of calcineurin via calcium–calmodulin interactions (Lim et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020). Activated calcineurin then dephosphorylates TFEB at key serine residues, resulting in its release from cytoplasmic retention complexes and enabling its translocation to the nucleus (Lim et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020). Once in the nucleus, TFEB binds to CLEAR network promoters, initiating the transcription of a suite of genes that are essential for lysosomal biogenesis, catabolic enzyme production, and enhanced autophagic flux (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Chen et al., 2021). This transcriptional upregulation leads to an increased lysosomal capacity, improved degradation of intracellular aggregates, and enhanced recycling of damaged organelles, which is particularly beneficial in the context of RPE cells that are burdened with the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E—byproducts of photoreceptor outer segment degradation (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). The specificity of MSL-7 for the calcium–calcineurin pathway is a significant advantage, as it circumvents typical mTOR-dependent pathways and thereby minimizes the risk of widespread metabolic disruption, offering a focused therapeutic effect on the autophagy–lysosomal system (Lim et al., 2018). In addition, the robustness of the mechanism is enhanced by the fact that TFEB activation has been shown to be beneficial in a number of models related to protein aggregation and cellular clearance, including neuronal and hepatic systems, thus providing a biochemical blueprint for its potential utility in RPE repair and dry AMD intervention (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nilotinib (Tasigna®, Novartis) is a synthetic small molecule inhibitor originally developed as a second‐generation BCR–ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor for the treatment of chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML). Developed through iterative medicinal chemistry optimization processes that sought to overcome resistance to first‐generation inhibitors such as imatinib, nilotinib is structurally designed to selectively bind the ATP-binding pocket of the c-Abl kinase, thereby inhibiting its catalytic activity (Karim et al., 2020). As a representative member of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), nilotinib falls into the class of targeted anticancer agents that have been widely used in oncology, with extensive preclinical and clinical experience in modulating aberrant kinase signaling pathways. The synthetic origins of nilotinib involve derivatization of earlier BCR–ABL inhibitors to improve potency and specificity, and its development has been a model for the design of targeted agents in diseases driven by kinase dysregulation (Karim et al., 2020). While its initial application has been in CML, its potent inhibition of c-Abl has attracted attention for repurposing in other conditions where this kinase plays a pathological role, including neurodegeneration and, as hypothesized here, dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Karim et al., 2020; Fowler et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Nilotinib has a well-documented clinical history as an FDA-approved therapeutic for CML, where its efficacy and safety profile have been established across numerous clinical trials and long-term follow-up studies. Over the past decade, repurposing efforts have extended into neurodegenerative diseases based on its ability to cross the blood–brain barrier (albeit at modest concentrations) and modulate pathogenic protein aggregation via autophagy enhancement. Preclinical studies in models of α-synucleinopathy, Parkinson’s disease, and Alzheimer’s disease have demonstrated that nilotinib can reduce toxic protein burden, improve autophagic clearance, and rescue neuronal survival by inhibiting c-Abl mediated pathways (Karim et al., 2020). This lack of prior clinical evaluation in the retinal domain represents both a gap in the evidence base and an opportunity for further translational research, building on the extensive safety and pharmacokinetic data already available from its oncological and neurodegenerative applications (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central mechanism of nilotinib is its inhibition of the aberrantly activated c-Abl tyrosine kinase. Under normal conditions, c-Abl regulates various cellular processes, including cell-cycle control, DNA repair, and stress responses. However, in pathological settings such as CML and certain neurodegenerative diseases, c-Abl becomes hyperactivated, leading to detrimental downstream effects including the activation of the tumor suppressor p53 via phosphorylation (Karim et al., 2020). In neurodegenerative models, c-Abl activation has been shown to interfere with autophagy, a critical intracellular degradation process, by upregulating p53 and inhibiting key autophagy initiators such as ULK1 and Beclin1 (Karim et al., 2020). Mechanistic studies in α-synucleinopathy models have demonstrated that nilotinib’s inhibition of c-Abl reduces the phosphorylation of p53 and decreases downstream mTORC1 signaling, thereby releasing autophagic blockades (Karim et al., 2020). Specifically, nilotinib treatment has been shown to enhance autophagic flux through increased conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II and reduced accumulation of the autophagy adaptor p62, indicating improved autophagosome formation and lysosomal clearance (Karim et al., 2020). Moreover, by inhibiting c-Abl, nilotinib alleviates the phosphorylation of ULK1 and enables its activation in an AMPK-dependent manner, which is critical for the initiation of autophagy; there is also emerging evidence that this inhibition may drive the formation or activation of the Beclin1 complex, further promoting autophagosome nucleation (Karim et al., 2020). Thus, nilotinib exerts a dual effect: it directly impedes the kinase activity of c-Abl while indirectly reactivating autophagic pathways that are otherwise suppressed by c-Abl’s pathological signaling via p53 and mTOR (Karim et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesized role of c-Abl in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, it is anticipated that nilotinib will have several beneficial effects in the context of dry AMD. In RPE cells, chronic oxidative stress and drusen-associated stressors are known to activate c-Abl, leading to the phosphorylation and inhibition of key autophagy regulators such as ULK1 and Beclin1. This interruption of autophagic flux is believed to contribute to lipofuscin accumulation, particularly of A2E, a toxic by-product implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Kim, Hwang, & Kwon, 2020; Karim et al., 2020). By inhibiting c-Abl, nilotinib should theoretically reverse this block, restore ULK1/Beclin1 activity, and re-establish effective autophagic clearance. In in vitro RPE cell assays that employ stresses such as A2E challenge and oxidative insults, nilotinib is expected to decrease the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, increase markers of autophagic flux such as LC3-II, and reduce p62 levels, thereby indicating enhanced lysosomal degradation (Kim, Hwang, & Kwon, 2020; Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024). Nilotinib represents a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration due to its well-characterized pharmacological profile, established safety through its use in CML, and promising mechanistic insights from neurodegeneration studies. One of the primary strengths of this candidate is its clear molecular mechanism: by inhibiting c-Abl, nilotinib has the potential to reverse the autophagy blockade mediated by pathological p53 activation and mTOR signaling, a mechanism that is plausibly relevant to the pathology observed in RPE cells under oxidative and drusen stress (Karim et al., 2020). First, despite the promising mechanistic data in neurodegenerative models, direct evidence for nilotinib’s efficacy in RPE cells and in models of dry AMD is currently lacking. A systematic search of clinical trial databases has revealed no registered trials for nilotinib in the context of AMD, which suggests that while preclinical data in other systems is robust, the translational leap to retinal applications remains uncharted (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Moreover, the molecular environment in the retina, particularly within the RPE, may differ in significant ways from neuronal tissues; factors such as differential expression patterns of autophagy regulators, variations in stress response signaling, and the unique barrier properties of the retina may influence nilotinib’s ultimate efficacy (Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024; Kim, Hwang, & Kwon, 2020).

Another potential concern is the specificity of nilotinib’s activity in the ocular environment. While its primary mechanism is through c-Abl inhibition, nilotinib has been documented to interact with other kinases (such as DDR1/DDR2) at low nanomolar concentrations (Fowler et al., 2019), which could lead to off-target effects that may be undesirable in the delicate architecture of the retina. These off-target interactions could potentially disrupt normal cellular processes within the retina, potentially exacerbating rather than ameliorating retinal degeneration if not carefully controlled (Fowler et al., 2019; Hussain et al., 2019). Additionally, while nilotinib’s safety profile has been demonstrated in systemic oncology settings, the safety and tolerability of chronic nilotinib administration directly affecting ocular tissues have yet to be thoroughly evaluated. Intraocular injections or other targeted delivery methods might be required to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina, and these routes carry their own risks of complications, including infection and retinal detachment (Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024).

In summary, nilotinib offers a conceptually appealing avenue for the treatment of dry AMD by targeting a clear molecular driver—c-Abl mediated autophagy dysfunction—that is implicated in the accumulation of toxic aggregates in RPE cells. The extensive preclinical data from neurodegenerative models provides a strong foundation that supports the hypothesis that nilotinib can restore autophagic flux by reactivating ULK1/Beclin1 function and reducing p53-mediated inhibition (Karim et al., 2020). The fact that nilotinib is already approved for human use and has well-characterized pharmacokinetics and safety data further enhances its attractiveness for repurposing. These challenges underscore the need for rigorous preclinical validation in RPE culture systems (e.g., using A2E challenge assays) and well-designed dry AMD animal models before advancing to clinical trials (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024).

Continued interdisciplinary research involving detailed biochemical studies, targeted delivery assessments, and in vivo pharmacodynamic evaluations will be critical to fully validate nilotinib’s therapeutic potential in the context of dry AMD.

As a member of a growing portfolio of HDAC6 inhibitors that originated from oncology and neurodegenerative research, Tubastatin A offers a well-documented chemical scaffold that has been optimized for both potency—with an IC₅₀ of approximately 15 nM—and favorable pharmacological properties including significant selectivity and in vivo tolerability (Wang, Wan, & Liu, 2018; Butler et al., 2010). Its synthetic origin and evolution from earlier molecules exemplify current trends in epigenetic drug discovery, where the focus is on generating compounds with high specificity toward individual HDAC family members to mitigate off-target effects while maintaining anticancer or neuroprotective efficacy (Batchu, Brijmohan, & Advani, 2016; Cosenza & Pozzi, 2018).

Therapeutic History: Tubastatin A has been extensively evaluated in preclinical studies within oncology and neurodegenerative disease frameworks, where HDAC6 has been implicated as a pivotal regulatory enzyme in both cancer cell survival and neuronal homeostasis (Simões-Pires, Bertrand, & Cuendet, 2017; Kalin & Bergman, 2013). In cancer research, Tubastatin A and its diarylamine- and hydroxamate-based analogs have been leveraged for their ability to selectively inhibit HDAC6-mediated deacetylation, thereby restoring acetylation of α-tubulin and counteracting aberrant cellular processes that are characteristic of malignant transformation. For instance, studies in multiple myeloma models have shown that selective inhibition of HDAC6 can create a therapeutic window that minimizes the collateral effects frequently observed with broad-spectrum HDAC inhibitors (Simões-Pires, Bertrand, & Cuendet, 2017). Parallel to its oncology applications, Tubastatin A has been assessed in a number of neuroprotective paradigms, where its action in increasing tubulin acetylation has been linked to the restoration of axonal transport mechanisms, mitochondrial dynamics, and overall neuronal integrity (Wang, Wan, & Liu, 2018; Butler et al., 2010). In rodent models of tauopathy and other neurodegenerative conditions, inhibition of HDAC6 with Tubastatin A has resulted in improvements in behavioral outcomes and the reduction of toxic protein aggregates, thereby lending credence to its molecular mechanism of action and efficacy in improving cellular autophagy (Kalin & Bergman, 2013; Selenica et al., 2014). Despite these promising preclinical results, there is as yet limited direct evidence of Tubastatin A being applied in models of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or in vivo studies specifically addressing retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cell dysfunction; however, several reports have highlighted the potential of HDAC6 inhibitors to modulate cellular processes, such as autophagosome–lysosome trafficking, that are directly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Kalin & Bergman, 2013; Buniello et al., 2025). Moreover, the favorable ADME profiles and established tolerability demonstrated by Tubastatin A in central nervous system (CNS) models suggest that repurposing this drug for ocular applications, while innovative, would build on a robust preclinical framework documented in other therapeutic areas (Shen et al., 2020b; Cosenza & Pozzi, 2018). Thus, from a therapeutic history perspective, Tubastatin A’s well-characterized profile in non-ocular systems and its mechanistic implications on autophagy present a compelling rationale for its evaluation as a candidate for dry AMD, while also noting that direct studies in retinal models remain a gap to be addressed in future investigations (Kalin & Bergman, 2013; Selenica et al., 2014).

Mechanism of Action: At the molecular level, Tubastatin A exerts its pharmacological effects by selectively inhibiting HDAC6, a cytoplasmic enzyme that is uniquely involved in the deacetylation of non-histone proteins. The principal substrate of HDAC6 is α-tubulin, a major component of the microtubule network, whose acetylation status is critical for maintaining microtubule stability and facilitating intracellular transport events (Wang, Wan, & Liu, 2018; Butler et al., 2010). By binding to the active site of HDAC6 through its hydroxamate zinc-binding group, Tubastatin A chelates the catalytic zinc ion and thereby blocks the deacetylation reaction, leading to an accumulation of acetylated α-tubulin (Butler et al., 2010; Shen & Kozikowski, 2020a). This increase in tubulin acetylation enhances the binding affinity of motor proteins—such as dynein—which are essential for driving the microtubule-dependent movement of vesicles and organelles (Shen & Kozikowski, 2020a; Shen et al., 2020b). In particular, the microtubule network plays a critical role in the movement of autophagosomes towards lysosomes, a process that is necessary for the maturation of autophagic vesicles and the subsequent degradation of cellular waste such as misfolded proteins and toxic lipid aggregates (Curcio et al., 2024; Shen & Kozikowski, 2020a). In neurodegenerative models, enhanced acetylation of microtubules by Tubastatin A has been shown to restore axonal transport as well as improve the clearance of abnormal tau proteins, thereby mitigating neurotoxicity (Kalin & Bergman, 2013; Selenica et al., 2014). This mechanism is of particular interest with respect to retinal pigment epithelium function in dry AMD because RPE cells are known to accumulate lipofuscin and A2E as a result of impaired autophagic flux under oxidative stress conditions (Kalin & Bergman, 2013; Buniello et al., 2025). The working hypothesis posits that HDAC6-mediated deacetylation of α-tubulin and autophagy-related proteins hampers the effective transport and fusion of autophagosomes with lysosomes; thus, by inhibiting HDAC6 with Tubastatin A, one can restore the acetylation status of these key proteins, enhance the motility of autophagosomes via improved dynein engagement, and ultimately promote the degradation of accumulated toxic substances (Shen & Kozikowski, 2020a; Olaoye et al., 2021). Furthermore, by selectively targeting HDAC6 without broadly inhibiting other histone deacetylases, Tubastatin A limits potential off-target effects that have historically been associated with non-selective HDAC inhibitors, thereby improving its safety margin and therapeutic index (Wang, Wan, & Liu, 2018; Butler et al., 2010). These molecular interactions collectively provide a plausible biochemical explanation for the observed neuroprotective and autophagy-enhancing effects of Tubastatin A in preclinical studies (Shen & Kozikowski, 2020a; Selenica et al., 2014).

Expected Effect: In the context of the proposed in vitro assays using induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, it is expected that treatment with Tubastatin A will lead to a measurable increase in the acetylation of α-tubulin and autophagy-related proteins such as LC3. This pharmacodynamic response is anticipated to facilitate improved recruitment and binding of the dynein motor complex to microtubules, thereby enhancing autophagosome transport toward lysosomes (Wang, Wan, & Liu, 2018; Kalin & Bergman, 2013). Under conditions of oxidative stress—a known contributory factor in dry AMD pathogenesis—RPE cells typically exhibit impaired autophagic flux, leading to the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, which are cytotoxic by-products of incomplete degradation pathways (Kalin & Bergman, 2013; Buniello et al., 2025). The hypothesis guiding the proposed studies is that by inhibiting HDAC6, Tubastatin A will “rescue” the autophagic pathway; increased microtubule acetylation is expected to enhance the velocity and efficiency of autophagosomal movement across the cytoskeletal network, promoting more efficient fusion with lysosomes and subsequent degradation of cellular debris (Shen & Kozikowski, 2020a). This effect can be quantitatively assessed by monitoring changes in LC3-II levels, the clearance of accumulated lipofuscin and A2E, and overall improvements in RPE cell viability and function in stressed cultures (Olaoye et al., 2021; Curcio et al., 2024). Moreover, given that HDAC6 is expressed in RPE cells, as evidenced by reports linking HDAC6 activity to both neural and epithelial pathologies, a targeted inhibition is hypothesized to directly ameliorate the intracellular trafficking bottlenecks that lead to the pathogenic buildup of waste products (Kalin & Bergman, 2013; Shen et al., 2020b). The expected cellular outcomes include restoration of autophagic flux, increased clearance of detrimental aggregates, reduction in oxidative stress markers, and the preservation or improvement of RPE cellular integrity, all of which are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis and mitigating progression in dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Shen & Kozikowski, 2020a). The compound’s documented in vivo tolerability and CNS penetration further support the notion that Tubastatin A, if capable of traversing ocular barriers, may exert similar beneficial effects within the retinal microenvironment (Wang, Wan, & Liu, 2018; Cosenza & Pozzi, 2018).

Overall Evaluation: In summary, Tubastatin A emerges as a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its well-established activity as a selective HDAC6 inhibitor, its robust synthetic accessibility, and its capacity to modulate autophagy-related processes. Strengths of Tubastatin A include its high potency (nanomolar IC₅₀), remarkable selectivity against other HDAC isoforms—which minimizes adverse off-target effects—and its documented ability to enhance acetylation of α-tubulin, thereby restoring microtubule stability and facilitating the transport of autophagic vesicles (Wang, Wan, & Liu, 2018; Butler et al., 2010). Its proven efficacy in models of neurodegeneration—in which similar cellular impairments of autophagosome trafficking and protein clearance are observed—adds further weight to the rationale for its application in RPE dysfunction associated with dry AMD (Kalin & Bergman, 2013; Selenica et al., 2014). The mechanistic hypothesis that HDAC6 inhibition can restore autophagosome–lysosome fusion and thereby accelerate the clearance of lipofuscin and A2E under oxidative conditions is supported by analogous findings in neuronal systems and emerging evidence from cellular assays (Kalin & Bergman, 2013; Shen & Kozikowski, 2020a). Additionally, Tubastatin A’s synthetic route, which permits rapid analog generation, its favorable ADME profiles, and the availability of preclinical safety data contribute significantly to its feasibility as a candidate for repurposing in ophthalmic applications (Shen & Kozikowski, 2020a; Cosenza & Pozzi, 2018).

Nevertheless, there remain some concerns and challenges that warrant attention. One of the primary weaknesses lies in the current paucity of direct evidence supporting Tubastatin A’s efficacy in ocular models or its ability to effectively penetrate the blood–retina barrier (Buniello et al., 2025; Kalin & Bergman, 2013). Furthermore, while the mechanistic data from neurodegenerative and oncological studies are compelling, translating these effects to the context of dry AMD will require careful verification in retinal-specific in vitro and in vivo systems. There is also the potential for unforeseen off-target effects in the unique microenvironment of the retina, where chronic oxidative stress and inflammatory cues may alter drug distribution or action (Shen & Kozikowski, 2020a). Additionally, although Tubastatin A’s selectivity minimizes inhibition of other HDAC isoforms, the role of non-HDAC6 deacetylation in maintaining retinal homeostasis is not fully elucidated; thus, comprehensive studies are needed to ensure that selective HDAC6 inhibition does not inadvertently disrupt other critical regulatory pathways within the RPE (Selenica et al., 2014; Butler et al., 2010).

In conclusion, Tubastatin A’s established profile as a potent, selective HDAC6 inhibitor—with its inherent ability to boost α-tubulin acetylation and thereby enhance autophagic trafficking—provides a strong scientific rationale for its further evaluation as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The candidate’s chemical and pharmacological attributes, which have been validated in parts through oncology and neurodegenerative research, align well with the proposed mechanism of action whereby impaired autophagosome–lysosome fusion contributes to RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. While pre-existing data primarily focus on its anti-tumor and neuroprotective roles, the mechanistic similarities shared between neuronal autophagic deficits and RPE deficits under oxidative stress conditions support the hypothesis that Tubastatin A may improve autophagic clearance of lipofuscin and A2E, thereby preserving RPE integrity (Kalin & Bergman, 2013; Buniello et al., 2025; Shen & Kozikowski, 2020a).

Moving forward, it will be critical to design rigorous preclinical studies using iPSC-derived RPE cells and appropriate animal models to evaluate the pharmacokinetics, ocular bioavailability, and long-term safety of Tubastatin A in the retinal setting. Such studies should incorporate detailed analyses of autophagy markers, lysosomal function, and the clearance kinetics of toxic aggregates under oxidative conditions. Additionally, investigations addressing potential off-target impacts and the capacity of Tubastatin A to penetrate ocular barriers will be essential to fully validate its repurposing for dry AMD. On balance, despite the current gaps in direct evidence for ocular applications, the strengths—including its targeted mechanism, robust safety profile in non-ocular systems, and ease of synthesis—position Tubastatin A as an attractive candidate for repurposing. It represents a scientifically sound and strategically promising approach to address the autophagic dysfunction underlying dry AMD, thereby meriting further investigation as part of an innovative therapeutic strategy (Wang, Wan, & Liu, 2018; Butler et al., 2010; Shen & Kozikowski, 2020a; Shen et al., 2020b).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
3,4-Dimethoxychalcone (DMC; Cayman Chemical catalog #CAY32002) is a small synthetic chalcone derivative belonging to the flavonoid family that has emerged in preclinical studies as a potent modulator of autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis. Derived through conventional organic synthetic routes involving aldol condensation reactions between appropriately substituted aromatic aldehydes and acetophenones, DMC exhibits a chalcone scaffold decorated with two methoxy groups that enhance its lipophilicity and potential bioactivity. Its chemical simplicity confers excellent drug‐like properties including favorable solubility, ease of synthesis, and established routes for chemical modification, thereby making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in indications such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) where manipulation of autophagic flux is desired (Gupta et al., 2023; Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2019). This compound has been investigated primarily for its ability to stimulate autophagy via transcription factor EB (TFEB) activation, a central regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy that is crucial for cellular clearance mechanisms in postmitotic cells including those in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, chalcones have been explored extensively in the context of longevity, anti‐cancer therapies, and metabolic regulation due to their versatile bioactivity profiles. DMC, in particular, has been reported to induce autophagy and promote lysosomal clearance in various cell types, with evidence emerging from studies in both mammalian cell culture systems and invertebrate models such as Caenorhabditis elegans. In one well‐documented study, DMC was shown to promote autophagic flux, leading to improved clearance of protein aggregates and damaged organelles without engaging the classical inhibition of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway—a mechanism that distinguishes it from rapalogs and may reduce associated immunosuppressive liabilities (Gupta et al., 2023; Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025). Although most of the pre‐clinical investigations using DMC have focused on its beneficial effects in the context of cardiac injury and age‐related neurodegeneration, these studies provide a strong rationale to consider its repurposing for diseases with an autophagy–lysosomal dysfunction component such as dry AMD (Lu et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2024). Furthermore, the literature on alternative TFEB activators—such as trehalose and rapamycin—in RPE cells and AMD models underscore the therapeutic promise of targeting TFEB, even though direct reports of DMC use in AMD models remain limited; instead, the extrapolation of its mechanism from other systems supports its evaluation in RPE-specific assays (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular underpinnings of DMC’s activity center on its capacity to induce TFEB dephosphorylation and promote its nuclear translocation in a manner that appears to bypass the canonical mTORC1 inhibitory pathway. Under homeostatic conditions, TFEB is phosphorylated by mTORC1, which sequesters it in the cytoplasm and limits its transcriptional regulation of genes involved in lysosomal and autophagy pathways. In stress situations, however, TFEB can undergo dephosphorylation—commonly mediated by the phosphatase calcineurin—allowing it to translocate into the nucleus, bind to coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) elements, and upregulate a broad array of lysosomal hydrolases, membrane proteins, and autophagy-related genes (Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2024). DMC is hypothesized to engage this calcineurin–TFEB axis directly, thereby inducing TFEB dephosphorylation without necessitating upstream mTOR inhibition. This mechanism is particularly advantageous given that it avoids the systemic immunosuppressive effects observed with rapamycin-like compounds that target mTOR directly (Gupta et al., 2023; Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025). Importantly, in primary neuronal and epithelial models, treatment with DMC has been reported to increase lysosome number, enhance cathepsin activity, and stimulate autophagic flux, all indicative of robust TFEB activation (Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025). On a biochemical level, the compound appears to trigger a signaling cascade that culminates in the dephosphorylation of key regulatory residues on TFEB, thereby relieving its cytoplasmic retention. Once in the nucleus, TFEB binds to CLEAR network promoters, simultaneously inducing genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis (e.g., LAMP1, Cathepsin D) as well as components of the autophagic machinery, which collectively enhance the cell’s capacity to clear damaged organelles and protein aggregates (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). Despite isolated reports suggesting that DMC might also exert mTOR inhibitory effects (as observed in certain cardiovascular studies), the prevailing data supporting an mTOR-independent activation of TFEB confers mechanistic specificity that is critical for its proposed use in dry AMD, where minimizing off-target immunosuppressive effects is essential (Lu et al., 2021; Gupta et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the RPE is burdened with the accumulation of photo-oxidized bisretinoids such as A2E and lipofuscin granules, which disrupt normal cellular function and eventually lead to cell death. The expected pharmacological effect of DMC in relevant assays centers on its capacity to induce TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE cells, consequently upregulating genes that drive lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic clearance. By enhancing the lysosomal degradation machinery, DMC would ideally promote the removal of toxic aggregates associated with oxidative stress and cellular aging, thus preserving RPE cell viability (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). In practical terms, when applied to human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells loaded with A2E, DMC is anticipated to reduce intracellular levels of this toxic byproduct along with the associated lipofuscin burden, thereby mitigating cellular stress and preventing cell death. Moreover, the activation of the TFEB pathway is expected to bolster additional cytoprotective responses, including the upregulation of cathepsin activity and other lysosomal hydrolases that contribute to a more efficient degradation of phagocytosed photoreceptor outer segment debris, a function that is crucial for RPE homeostasis (Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2025). The enhanced autophagic flux facilitated by DMC is also likely to intersect with antioxidative pathways, potentially engaging the NRF2/KEAP1 axis, which further reinforces cellular defenses against oxidative damage—a major contributing factor in AMD pathogenesis (Falcão et al., 2025). Thus, in preclinical assays and future in vivo dry AMD models, DMC should manifest as a compound that not only clears deleterious aggregates but also restores overall lysosomal function and cellular homeostasis without the deleterious side effects often associated with mTOR inhibitors (Falcão et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
The evaluation of 3,4-Dimethoxychalcone (DMC) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD presents several compelling strengths alongside certain challenges that must be critically addressed through further research. Among the primary strengths is DMC’s ability to modulate the TFEB pathway in a manner that is claimed to be independent of mTOR inhibition. This mTOR-independent mechanism offers a significant advantage over traditional mTOR inhibitors such as rapamycin, as it theoretically minimizes the risk of systemic immunosuppression and other mTOR-related side effects while still harnessing the potent autophagy-enhancing and lysosome-boosting effects mediated by TFEB (Gupta et al., 2023; Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025). Additionally, the favorable physicochemical properties of DMC—including its small molecular size, established synthetic routes, and amenable solubility profile—facilitate its potential development as a therapeutic agent for ocular applications where drug delivery and tissue penetration into the retina are critical considerations (Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2019). The compound’s demonstrated capacity to increase lysosomal number, stimulate cathepsin activity, and elevate autophagic flux in other cell types further supports its viability as a candidate for clearing chronic intracellular accumulations characteristic of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024).

From a biochemical standpoint, the targeted activation of the calcineurin–TFEB axis by DMC aligns well with current therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring cellular homeostasis in degenerative diseases. By promoting nuclear translocation of TFEB without broadly inhibiting mTOR, DMC could specifically upregulate genes involved not only in lysosomal biogenesis but also in general autophagic processing, thereby addressing both the accumulation of toxic aggregates (such as A2E and lipofuscin granules) and the compromised cellular clearance pathways in the RPE (Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2025). Moreover, the potential engagement of downstream protective pathways—possibly including cross-talk with the NRF2-mediated antioxidative response—accentuates DMC’s promise as a dual-action compound that simultaneously mitigates oxidative stress and improves proteostasis in retinal cells (Falcão et al., 2025).

However, notable weaknesses and uncertainties remain that merit cautious consideration. First, although DMC has been shown in various experimental models to enhance autophagic and lysosomal functions, direct evidence supporting its efficacy specifically in RPE cells or in animal models of dry AMD is currently limited. Most reports detailing its mechanism originate from studies in cardiac and neuronal contexts, leaving a gap in replication and validation within ocular tissues. This translational gap necessitates rigorous preclinical testing using human iPSC-derived RPE cells and established dry AMD animal models to confirm that the TFEB activation observed in other systems translates effectively to the RPE environment (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Another challenge lies in the mechanistic ambiguity surrounding whether DMC acts entirely in an mTOR-independent fashion. While several studies extol its ability to activate TFEB without direct mTOR suppression—thus avoiding the side effects of mTOR inhibitors—other reports have suggested that related compounds may exhibit some degree of mTOR inhibition, which could potentially complicate the pharmacological profile of DMC (Lu et al., 2021; Gupta et al., 2023). This discrepancy underscores the need for detailed mechanistic studies using RPE-specific models to delineate the precise signaling cascades engaged by DMC, including assessment of calcineurin activity, TFEB dephosphorylation status, and the downstream transcriptional activation of CLEAR network genes (Gupta et al., 2023; Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025).

Furthermore, while the proposed benefits of enhanced autophagic flux and lysosomal biogenesis are clear, the potential for off-target effects, long-term toxicity, and issues related to drug delivery in the ocular environment must be thoroughly evaluated. Ocular pharmacokinetics can differ markedly from systemic profiles, and the challenges associated with ensuring adequate retinal bioavailability—particularly in the context of the blood–retina barrier—should not be underestimated. In addition, the possible influence of DMC on other cellular pathways, such as those governing mitochondrial function and metabolic regulation, may introduce additional layers of complexity when considering chronic treatment regimens for a slowly progressing condition like dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024; Gupta et al., 2023).

In terms of translational potential, DMC’s repurposing for dry AMD would benefit from head-to-head comparisons with other TFEB activators that have been studied in RPE cells, such as trehalose and rapamycin. While these agents have already demonstrated beneficial effects on lipofuscin clearance and oxidative stress reduction in experimental settings, the distinct advantage of DMC may reside in its ability to engage the TFEB pathway without the collateral effects on mTOR, thereby offering a cleaner safety profile. Nevertheless, systematic studies comparing dose–response relationships, pharmacodynamics, and potential synergistic effects with other autophagy modulators will be essential prior to advancing DMC into clinical development (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

An additional consideration is the heterogeneity present among dry AMD patients. Genetic factors, such as the presence of the CFH Y402H variant, and environmental stressors can influence the progression and severity of RPE degeneration. It will be critical to establish whether DMC’s TFEB-mediated effects are robust across different RPE phenotypes and whether any differential responses may necessitate patient stratification in future clinical trials. The potential for DMC to rescue autophagy-related gene expression and lysosomal function, as suggested by similar findings with TFEB activators in other models, provides a strong impetus for such studies, but careful experimental design will be paramount (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Overall, the repurposing of 3,4-Dimethoxychalcone as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is supported by a solid rationale predicated on its capacity to activate TFEB and enhance autophagic and lysosomal processes in a manner that is potentially independent of mTOR inhibition. Its chemical properties, ease of synthesis, and preliminary evidence from related experimental models collectively argue in favor of its evaluation in RPE-specific assays and animal models of dry AMD. At the same time, key challenges—including the need for clear demonstration of its mTOR-independent mechanism in ocular tissues, comprehensive toxicity profiling, and optimization of drug delivery strategies—must be addressed in subsequent preclinical studies. Given the robust body of literature supporting the critical role of TFEB in maintaining RPE health and mitigating lipofuscin accumulation, DMC stands out as a promising candidate that could offer a novel approach to the treatment of dry AMD, provided that future research confirms its efficacy and safety in the retinal context (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024; Gupta et al., 2023).

In conclusion, the current comprehensive literature review suggests that 3,4-Dimethoxychalcone exhibits significant potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Its unique mechanism of inducing TFEB dephosphorylation and promoting lysosomal biogenesis—thereby enhancing autophagic clearance of photo-oxidized bisretinoids and lipofuscin granules—addresses a fundamental pathogenic process in RPE degeneration. While the preclinical evidence on DMC from non-ocular models is compelling, rigorous validation in RPE-specific systems is essential to definitively establish its role in modulating autophagy and improving retinal cell survival. The strengths of DMC in terms of mechanistic specificity, favorable pharmacological properties, and avoidance of mTOR-related side effects make it a strong candidate for further development, while the challenges associated with direct translation to ocular models underscore the need for carefully designed preclinical studies. As such, the proposed direction for our drug development effort should focus on detailed in vitro assays using human iPSC-derived RPE cells, followed by in vivo evaluation in dry AMD animal models, to fully delineate the therapeutic potential and safety profile of DMC for clinical application in dry AMD (Gupta et al., 2023; Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nilotinib (Tasigna®, Novartis) is a synthetic small molecule inhibitor originally developed as a second‐generation BCR–ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor for the treatment of chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML). Developed through iterative medicinal chemistry optimization processes that sought to overcome resistance to first‐generation inhibitors such as imatinib, nilotinib is structurally designed to selectively bind the ATP-binding pocket of the c-Abl kinase, thereby inhibiting its catalytic activity (Karim et al., 2020). As a representative member of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), nilotinib falls into the class of targeted anticancer agents that have been widely used in oncology, with extensive preclinical and clinical experience in modulating aberrant kinase signaling pathways. The synthetic origins of nilotinib involve derivatization of earlier BCR–ABL inhibitors to improve potency and specificity, and its development has been a model for the design of targeted agents in diseases driven by kinase dysregulation (Karim et al., 2020). While its initial application has been in CML, its potent inhibition of c-Abl has attracted attention for repurposing in other conditions where this kinase plays a pathological role, including neurodegeneration and, as hypothesized here, dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Karim et al., 2020; Fowler et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Nilotinib has a well-documented clinical history as an FDA-approved therapeutic for CML, where its efficacy and safety profile have been established across numerous clinical trials and long-term follow-up studies. Over the past decade, repurposing efforts have extended into neurodegenerative diseases based on its ability to cross the blood–brain barrier (albeit at modest concentrations) and modulate pathogenic protein aggregation via autophagy enhancement. Preclinical studies in models of α-synucleinopathy, Parkinson’s disease, and Alzheimer’s disease have demonstrated that nilotinib can reduce toxic protein burden, improve autophagic clearance, and rescue neuronal survival by inhibiting c-Abl mediated pathways (Karim et al., 2020). Despite these promising findings in neurological contexts, a systematic search of clinical trial databases reveals that nilotinib has not yet been directly investigated in dry AMD or related retinal degenerative conditions (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). This lack of prior clinical evaluation in the retinal domain represents both a gap in the evidence base and an opportunity for further translational research, building on the extensive safety and pharmacokinetic data already available from its oncological and neurodegenerative applications (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central mechanism of nilotinib is its inhibition of the aberrantly activated c-Abl tyrosine kinase. Under normal conditions, c-Abl regulates various cellular processes, including cell-cycle control, DNA repair, and stress responses. However, in pathological settings such as CML and certain neurodegenerative diseases, c-Abl becomes hyperactivated, leading to detrimental downstream effects including the activation of the tumor suppressor p53 via phosphorylation (Karim et al., 2020). In neurodegenerative models, c-Abl activation has been shown to interfere with autophagy, a critical intracellular degradation process, by upregulating p53 and inhibiting key autophagy initiators such as ULK1 and Beclin1 (Karim et al., 2020). Mechanistic studies in α-synucleinopathy models have demonstrated that nilotinib’s inhibition of c-Abl reduces the phosphorylation of p53 and decreases downstream mTORC1 signaling, thereby releasing autophagic blockades (Karim et al., 2020). Specifically, nilotinib treatment has been shown to enhance autophagic flux through increased conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II and reduced accumulation of the autophagy adaptor p62, indicating improved autophagosome formation and lysosomal clearance (Karim et al., 2020). Moreover, by inhibiting c-Abl, nilotinib alleviates the phosphorylation of ULK1 and enables its activation in an AMPK-dependent manner, which is critical for the initiation of autophagy; there is also emerging evidence that this inhibition may drive the formation or activation of the Beclin1 complex, further promoting autophagosome nucleation (Karim et al., 2020). Thus, nilotinib exerts a dual effect: it directly impedes the kinase activity of c-Abl while indirectly reactivating autophagic pathways that are otherwise suppressed by c-Abl’s pathological signaling via p53 and mTOR (Karim et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesized role of c-Abl in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, it is anticipated that nilotinib will have several beneficial effects in the context of dry AMD. In RPE cells, chronic oxidative stress and drusen-associated stressors are known to activate c-Abl, leading to the phosphorylation and inhibition of key autophagy regulators such as ULK1 and Beclin1. This interruption of autophagic flux is believed to contribute to lipofuscin accumulation, particularly of A2E, a toxic by-product implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Kim, Hwang, & Kwon, 2020; Karim et al., 2020). By inhibiting c-Abl, nilotinib should theoretically reverse this block, restore ULK1/Beclin1 activity, and re-establish effective autophagic clearance. In in vitro RPE cell assays that employ stresses such as A2E challenge and oxidative insults, nilotinib is expected to decrease the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, increase markers of autophagic flux such as LC3-II, and reduce p62 levels, thereby indicating enhanced lysosomal degradation (Kim, Hwang, & Kwon, 2020; Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024). With improved autophagic processing, the cellular homeostasis within RPE cells should be restored, thereby preventing the degenerative changes that contribute to drusen formation and the overall progression of dry AMD. Furthermore, animal studies in neurodegenerative models have shown that nilotinib can lead to delayed onset of clinical symptoms and improved cell survival, lending support to the potential translational value of these mechanisms in the retinal environment (Karim et al., 2020). It is important to note that while supportive mechanistic evidence exists from neurodegeneration research, direct experimental validation of nilotinib’s impact on RPE autophagy and lipofuscin clearance in dry AMD-specific models remains to be performed (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
Nilotinib represents a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration due to its well-characterized pharmacological profile, established safety through its use in CML, and promising mechanistic insights from neurodegeneration studies. One of the primary strengths of this candidate is its clear molecular mechanism: by inhibiting c-Abl, nilotinib has the potential to reverse the autophagy blockade mediated by pathological p53 activation and mTOR signaling, a mechanism that is plausibly relevant to the pathology observed in RPE cells under oxidative and drusen stress (Karim et al., 2020). The existing literature strongly supports the notion that c-Abl plays a pivotal role in autophagy regulation, with multiple studies demonstrating that its inhibition leads to enhanced autophagic clearance of toxic protein aggregates in neuronal models (Karim et al., 2020; Kim, Hwang, & Kwon, 2020). This mechanistic similarity is particularly encouraging given that autophagic dysfunction and accumulation of cellular debris such as lipofuscin (and its A2E component) are central to the progression of dry AMD (Kim, Hwang, & Kwon, 2020; Karim et al., 2020).

Another strength is the translational potential based on nilotinib’s pharmacokinetic profile. Despite challenges often associated with drug delivery to the central nervous system and ocular tissues, nilotinib has demonstrated the ability to cross the blood–brain barrier at pharmacologically relevant doses, suggesting that similar (albeit low-dose) penetration of the blood–retina barrier might be achievable. This is supported by the documented systemic administration protocols in preclinical neurodegeneration models where nilotinib exhibited biological activity in brain tissues (Karim et al., 2020), and by extension, such dosing strategies may be adapted for ocular tissues. The fact that nilotinib is already FDA-approved means that its safety profile, dosing parameters, and potential side effects are well understood, which significantly reduces the risk and accelerates the timeline for repurposing in a new indication (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024).

However, there are several weaknesses and challenges that must be acknowledged. First, despite the promising mechanistic data in neurodegenerative models, direct evidence for nilotinib’s efficacy in RPE cells and in models of dry AMD is currently lacking. A systematic search of clinical trial databases has revealed no registered trials for nilotinib in the context of AMD, which suggests that while preclinical data in other systems is robust, the translational leap to retinal applications remains uncharted (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Moreover, the molecular environment in the retina, particularly within the RPE, may differ in significant ways from neuronal tissues; factors such as differential expression patterns of autophagy regulators, variations in stress response signaling, and the unique barrier properties of the retina may influence nilotinib’s ultimate efficacy (Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024; Kim, Hwang, & Kwon, 2020).

Another potential concern is the specificity of nilotinib’s activity in the ocular environment. While its primary mechanism is through c-Abl inhibition, nilotinib has been documented to interact with other kinases (such as DDR1/DDR2) at low nanomolar concentrations (Fowler et al., 2019), which could lead to off-target effects that may be undesirable in the delicate architecture of the retina. These off-target interactions could potentially disrupt normal cellular processes within the retina, potentially exacerbating rather than ameliorating retinal degeneration if not carefully controlled (Fowler et al., 2019; Hussain et al., 2019). Additionally, while nilotinib’s safety profile has been demonstrated in systemic oncology settings, the safety and tolerability of chronic nilotinib administration directly affecting ocular tissues have yet to be thoroughly evaluated. Intraocular injections or other targeted delivery methods might be required to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina, and these routes carry their own risks of complications, including infection and retinal detachment (Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024).

In summary, nilotinib offers a conceptually appealing avenue for the treatment of dry AMD by targeting a clear molecular driver—c-Abl mediated autophagy dysfunction—that is implicated in the accumulation of toxic aggregates in RPE cells. The extensive preclinical data from neurodegenerative models provides a strong foundation that supports the hypothesis that nilotinib can restore autophagic flux by reactivating ULK1/Beclin1 function and reducing p53-mediated inhibition (Karim et al., 2020). The fact that nilotinib is already approved for human use and has well-characterized pharmacokinetics and safety data further enhances its attractiveness for repurposing. Nonetheless, significant hurdles remain, most notably the absence of direct evidence in retinal models, potential differences in drug permeability and target engagement in RPE cells, and the risk of off-target effects in ocular tissues. These challenges underscore the need for rigorous preclinical validation in RPE culture systems (e.g., using A2E challenge assays) and well-designed dry AMD animal models before advancing to clinical trials (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024).

Overall, given its mechanistic rationale, previous efficacy in related neurodegenerative contexts, and favorable safety profile in oncology, nilotinib stands out as a promising candidate for further exploration as a treatment for dry AMD. Its repurposing offers a high translational value with the potential to address a major unmet medical need, provided that future studies can confirm its ability to cross the blood–retina barrier, restore autophagic processing in RPE cells, and ultimately prevent RPE degeneration without incurring significant ocular toxicity (Fowler et al., 2019; Karim et al., 2020). Continued interdisciplinary research involving detailed biochemical studies, targeted delivery assessments, and in vivo pharmacodynamic evaluations will be critical to fully validate nilotinib’s therapeutic potential in the context of dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
3,4-Dimethoxychalcone (DMC; Cayman Chemical catalog #CAY32002) is a small synthetic chalcone derivative belonging to the flavonoid family that has emerged in preclinical studies as a potent modulator of autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis. Derived through conventional organic synthetic routes involving aldol condensation reactions between appropriately substituted aromatic aldehydes and acetophenones, DMC exhibits a chalcone scaffold decorated with two methoxy groups that enhance its lipophilicity and potential bioactivity. Its chemical simplicity confers excellent drug‐like properties including favorable solubility, ease of synthesis, and established routes for chemical modification, thereby making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in indications such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) where manipulation of autophagic flux is desired (Gupta et al., 2023; Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2019). This compound has been investigated primarily for its ability to stimulate autophagy via transcription factor EB (TFEB) activation, a central regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy that is crucial for cellular clearance mechanisms in postmitotic cells including those in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, chalcones have been explored extensively in the context of longevity, anti‐cancer therapies, and metabolic regulation due to their versatile bioactivity profiles. DMC, in particular, has been reported to induce autophagy and promote lysosomal clearance in various cell types, with evidence emerging from studies in both mammalian cell culture systems and invertebrate models such as Caenorhabditis elegans. In one well‐documented study, DMC was shown to promote autophagic flux, leading to improved clearance of protein aggregates and damaged organelles without engaging the classical inhibition of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway—a mechanism that distinguishes it from rapalogs and may reduce associated immunosuppressive liabilities (Gupta et al., 2023; Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025). Although most of the pre‐clinical investigations using DMC have focused on its beneficial effects in the context of cardiac injury and age‐related neurodegeneration, these studies provide a strong rationale to consider its repurposing for diseases with an autophagy–lysosomal dysfunction component such as dry AMD (Lu et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2024). Furthermore, the literature on alternative TFEB activators—such as trehalose and rapamycin—in RPE cells and AMD models underscore the therapeutic promise of targeting TFEB, even though direct reports of DMC use in AMD models remain limited; instead, the extrapolation of its mechanism from other systems supports its evaluation in RPE-specific assays (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular underpinnings of DMC’s activity center on its capacity to induce TFEB dephosphorylation and promote its nuclear translocation in a manner that appears to bypass the canonical mTORC1 inhibitory pathway. Under homeostatic conditions, TFEB is phosphorylated by mTORC1, which sequesters it in the cytoplasm and limits its transcriptional regulation of genes involved in lysosomal and autophagy pathways. In stress situations, however, TFEB can undergo dephosphorylation—commonly mediated by the phosphatase calcineurin—allowing it to translocate into the nucleus, bind to coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) elements, and upregulate a broad array of lysosomal hydrolases, membrane proteins, and autophagy-related genes (Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2024). DMC is hypothesized to engage this calcineurin–TFEB axis directly, thereby inducing TFEB dephosphorylation without necessitating upstream mTOR inhibition. This mechanism is particularly advantageous given that it avoids the systemic immunosuppressive effects observed with rapamycin-like compounds that target mTOR directly (Gupta et al., 2023; Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025). Importantly, in primary neuronal and epithelial models, treatment with DMC has been reported to increase lysosome number, enhance cathepsin activity, and stimulate autophagic flux, all indicative of robust TFEB activation (Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025). On a biochemical level, the compound appears to trigger a signaling cascade that culminates in the dephosphorylation of key regulatory residues on TFEB, thereby relieving its cytoplasmic retention. Once in the nucleus, TFEB binds to CLEAR network promoters, simultaneously inducing genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis (e.g., LAMP1, Cathepsin D) as well as components of the autophagic machinery, which collectively enhance the cell’s capacity to clear damaged organelles and protein aggregates (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). Despite isolated reports suggesting that DMC might also exert mTOR inhibitory effects (as observed in certain cardiovascular studies), the prevailing data supporting an mTOR-independent activation of TFEB confers mechanistic specificity that is critical for its proposed use in dry AMD, where minimizing off-target immunosuppressive effects is essential (Lu et al., 2021; Gupta et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the RPE is burdened with the accumulation of photo-oxidized bisretinoids such as A2E and lipofuscin granules, which disrupt normal cellular function and eventually lead to cell death. The expected pharmacological effect of DMC in relevant assays centers on its capacity to induce TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE cells, consequently upregulating genes that drive lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic clearance. By enhancing the lysosomal degradation machinery, DMC would ideally promote the removal of toxic aggregates associated with oxidative stress and cellular aging, thus preserving RPE cell viability (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). In practical terms, when applied to human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells loaded with A2E, DMC is anticipated to reduce intracellular levels of this toxic byproduct along with the associated lipofuscin burden, thereby mitigating cellular stress and preventing cell death. Moreover, the activation of the TFEB pathway is expected to bolster additional cytoprotective responses, including the upregulation of cathepsin activity and other lysosomal hydrolases that contribute to a more efficient degradation of phagocytosed photoreceptor outer segment debris, a function that is crucial for RPE homeostasis (Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2025). The enhanced autophagic flux facilitated by DMC is also likely to intersect with antioxidative pathways, potentially engaging the NRF2/KEAP1 axis, which further reinforces cellular defenses against oxidative damage—a major contributing factor in AMD pathogenesis (Falcão et al., 2025). Thus, in preclinical assays and future in vivo dry AMD models, DMC should manifest as a compound that not only clears deleterious aggregates but also restores overall lysosomal function and cellular homeostasis without the deleterious side effects often associated with mTOR inhibitors (Falcão et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
The evaluation of 3,4-Dimethoxychalcone (DMC) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD presents several compelling strengths alongside certain challenges that must be critically addressed through further research. Among the primary strengths is DMC’s ability to modulate the TFEB pathway in a manner that is claimed to be independent of mTOR inhibition. This mTOR-independent mechanism offers a significant advantage over traditional mTOR inhibitors such as rapamycin, as it theoretically minimizes the risk of systemic immunosuppression and other mTOR-related side effects while still harnessing the potent autophagy-enhancing and lysosome-boosting effects mediated by TFEB (Gupta et al., 2023; Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025). Additionally, the favorable physicochemical properties of DMC—including its small molecular size, established synthetic routes, and amenable solubility profile—facilitate its potential development as a therapeutic agent for ocular applications where drug delivery and tissue penetration into the retina are critical considerations (Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2019). The compound’s demonstrated capacity to increase lysosomal number, stimulate cathepsin activity, and elevate autophagic flux in other cell types further supports its viability as a candidate for clearing chronic intracellular accumulations characteristic of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024).

From a biochemical standpoint, the targeted activation of the calcineurin–TFEB axis by DMC aligns well with current therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring cellular homeostasis in degenerative diseases. By promoting nuclear translocation of TFEB without broadly inhibiting mTOR, DMC could specifically upregulate genes involved not only in lysosomal biogenesis but also in general autophagic processing, thereby addressing both the accumulation of toxic aggregates (such as A2E and lipofuscin granules) and the compromised cellular clearance pathways in the RPE (Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2025). Moreover, the potential engagement of downstream protective pathways—possibly including cross-talk with the NRF2-mediated antioxidative response—accentuates DMC’s promise as a dual-action compound that simultaneously mitigates oxidative stress and improves proteostasis in retinal cells (Falcão et al., 2025).

However, notable weaknesses and uncertainties remain that merit cautious consideration. First, although DMC has been shown in various experimental models to enhance autophagic and lysosomal functions, direct evidence supporting its efficacy specifically in RPE cells or in animal models of dry AMD is currently limited. Most reports detailing its mechanism originate from studies in cardiac and neuronal contexts, leaving a gap in replication and validation within ocular tissues. This translational gap necessitates rigorous preclinical testing using human iPSC-derived RPE cells and established dry AMD animal models to confirm that the TFEB activation observed in other systems translates effectively to the RPE environment (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Another challenge lies in the mechanistic ambiguity surrounding whether DMC acts entirely in an mTOR-independent fashion. While several studies extol its ability to activate TFEB without direct mTOR suppression—thus avoiding the side effects of mTOR inhibitors—other reports have suggested that related compounds may exhibit some degree of mTOR inhibition, which could potentially complicate the pharmacological profile of DMC (Lu et al., 2021; Gupta et al., 2023). This discrepancy underscores the need for detailed mechanistic studies using RPE-specific models to delineate the precise signaling cascades engaged by DMC, including assessment of calcineurin activity, TFEB dephosphorylation status, and the downstream transcriptional activation of CLEAR network genes (Gupta et al., 2023; Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025).

Furthermore, while the proposed benefits of enhanced autophagic flux and lysosomal biogenesis are clear, the potential for off-target effects, long-term toxicity, and issues related to drug delivery in the ocular environment must be thoroughly evaluated. Ocular pharmacokinetics can differ markedly from systemic profiles, and the challenges associated with ensuring adequate retinal bioavailability—particularly in the context of the blood–retina barrier—should not be underestimated. In addition, the possible influence of DMC on other cellular pathways, such as those governing mitochondrial function and metabolic regulation, may introduce additional layers of complexity when considering chronic treatment regimens for a slowly progressing condition like dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024; Gupta et al., 2023).

In terms of translational potential, DMC’s repurposing for dry AMD would benefit from head-to-head comparisons with other TFEB activators that have been studied in RPE cells, such as trehalose and rapamycin. While these agents have already demonstrated beneficial effects on lipofuscin clearance and oxidative stress reduction in experimental settings, the distinct advantage of DMC may reside in its ability to engage the TFEB pathway without the collateral effects on mTOR, thereby offering a cleaner safety profile. Nevertheless, systematic studies comparing dose–response relationships, pharmacodynamics, and potential synergistic effects with other autophagy modulators will be essential prior to advancing DMC into clinical development (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

An additional consideration is the heterogeneity present among dry AMD patients. Genetic factors, such as the presence of the CFH Y402H variant, and environmental stressors can influence the progression and severity of RPE degeneration. It will be critical to establish whether DMC’s TFEB-mediated effects are robust across different RPE phenotypes and whether any differential responses may necessitate patient stratification in future clinical trials. The potential for DMC to rescue autophagy-related gene expression and lysosomal function, as suggested by similar findings with TFEB activators in other models, provides a strong impetus for such studies, but careful experimental design will be paramount (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Overall, the repurposing of 3,4-Dimethoxychalcone as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is supported by a solid rationale predicated on its capacity to activate TFEB and enhance autophagic and lysosomal processes in a manner that is potentially independent of mTOR inhibition. Its chemical properties, ease of synthesis, and preliminary evidence from related experimental models collectively argue in favor of its evaluation in RPE-specific assays and animal models of dry AMD. At the same time, key challenges—including the need for clear demonstration of its mTOR-independent mechanism in ocular tissues, comprehensive toxicity profiling, and optimization of drug delivery strategies—must be addressed in subsequent preclinical studies. Given the robust body of literature supporting the critical role of TFEB in maintaining RPE health and mitigating lipofuscin accumulation, DMC stands out as a promising candidate that could offer a novel approach to the treatment of dry AMD, provided that future research confirms its efficacy and safety in the retinal context (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024; Gupta et al., 2023).

In conclusion, the current comprehensive literature review suggests that 3,4-Dimethoxychalcone exhibits significant potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Its unique mechanism of inducing TFEB dephosphorylation and promoting lysosomal biogenesis—thereby enhancing autophagic clearance of photo-oxidized bisretinoids and lipofuscin granules—addresses a fundamental pathogenic process in RPE degeneration. While the preclinical evidence on DMC from non-ocular models is compelling, rigorous validation in RPE-specific systems is essential to definitively establish its role in modulating autophagy and improving retinal cell survival. The strengths of DMC in terms of mechanistic specificity, favorable pharmacological properties, and avoidance of mTOR-related side effects make it a strong candidate for further development, while the challenges associated with direct translation to ocular models underscore the need for carefully designed preclinical studies. As such, the proposed direction for our drug development effort should focus on detailed in vitro assays using human iPSC-derived RPE cells, followed by in vivo evaluation in dry AMD animal models, to fully delineate the therapeutic potential and safety profile of DMC for clinical application in dry AMD (Gupta et al., 2023; Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
MSL-7 is a potent, synthetic small‐molecule activator of transcription factor EB (TFEB) that was discovered through high‐content screening methodologies and is commercially available (Cayman Chemical catalog #14818). This candidate belongs to a novel class of autophagy enhancers that exploit the calcium–calcineurin signaling pathway rather than the classical mTOR inhibition mechanism to induce nuclear translocation of TFEB (Lim et al., 2018). Unlike many mTOR inhibitors that produce a broader range of kinase and metabolic inhibition with considerable off‐target effects, MSL-7 is designed to selectively elevate cytosolic calcium in target cells, leading to the activation of the phosphatase calcineurin and subsequent dephosphorylation of TFEB (Lim et al., 2018). Subsequently, dephosphorylated TFEB translocates to the nucleus, where it binds to coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) motifs and activates the transcription of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Chen et al., 2021). As a member of the small-molecule TFEB activators, MSL-7 represents a targeted therapeutic approach that has been primarily studied for metabolic disorders and neurodegenerative conditions and now is being considered for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) due to the critical role of lysosomal dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) pathology (Lim et al., 2018; Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of molecules that modulate TFEB activity spans multiple disease areas, including metabolic syndrome, neurodegeneration, and lysosomal storage disorders. MSL-7 itself has been evaluated in preclinical models for metabolic syndrome, showing promising metabolic improvements via its activation of the calcium–calcineurin–TFEB axis (Lim et al., 2018). In these studies, MSL-7 reversed metabolic changes through enhanced autophagic flux and improved lysosomal clearance, setting a precedent for its application in diseases where accumulation of toxic aggregates is central to pathology (Lim et al., 2018). Although MSL-7 has not been directly used for the treatment of dry AMD in clinical studies, considerable evidence from biochemical and cellular studies supports the concept that activation of TFEB can ameliorate age-dependent RPE dysfunction by promoting the clearance of lipofuscin and other toxic aggregates (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025). Prior studies of other TFEB activators—such as trehalose, which has been shown to enhance autophagic clearance in RPE cells—provide a robust rationale for the application of MSL-7 in retinal degenerative models (Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Moreover, the involvement of the autophagy–lysosomal network in maintaining retinal health and its impairment in AMD have been well documented, suggesting that strategies to enhance autophagic clearance via TFEB activation are both mechanistically sound and therapeutically appealing (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism of MSL-7 centers on its ability to modulate intracellular calcium dynamics, which is critical for the activation of the phosphatase calcineurin. Under physiological conditions, TFEB remains phosphorylated and sequestered in the cytoplasm by the action of mTORC1 and possibly other kinases; however, when MSL-7 is applied, it elevates cytosolic calcium levels specifically in RPE cells, thereby leading to the activation of calcineurin via calcium–calmodulin interactions (Lim et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020). Activated calcineurin then dephosphorylates TFEB at key serine residues, resulting in its release from cytoplasmic retention complexes and enabling its translocation to the nucleus (Lim et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020). Once in the nucleus, TFEB binds to CLEAR network promoters, initiating the transcription of a suite of genes that are essential for lysosomal biogenesis, catabolic enzyme production, and enhanced autophagic flux (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Chen et al., 2021). This transcriptional upregulation leads to an increased lysosomal capacity, improved degradation of intracellular aggregates, and enhanced recycling of damaged organelles, which is particularly beneficial in the context of RPE cells that are burdened with the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E—byproducts of photoreceptor outer segment degradation (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). The specificity of MSL-7 for the calcium–calcineurin pathway is a significant advantage, as it circumvents typical mTOR-dependent pathways and thereby minimizes the risk of widespread metabolic disruption, offering a focused therapeutic effect on the autophagy–lysosomal system (Lim et al., 2018). In addition, the robustness of the mechanism is enhanced by the fact that TFEB activation has been shown to be beneficial in a number of models related to protein aggregation and cellular clearance, including neuronal and hepatic systems, thus providing a biochemical blueprint for its potential utility in RPE repair and dry AMD intervention (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

When applied to human iPSC-derived RPE models of dry AMD that exhibit lipofuscin accumulation, MSL-7 is hypothesized to restore cellular homeostasis by robustly enhancing autophagic flux and lysosomal biogenesis. The expected cellular effects include an elevated clearance of lipofuscin-like granules and A2E, which are hallmark toxic deposits in RPE cells and are directly implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).
