Moreover, the augmentation of autophagic capacity is expected not only to mitigate the deleterious buildup of cellular waste but also to reduce pro-inflammatory signaling and oxidative stress—a dual mechanism that could slow disease progression and preserve visual acuity in patients with dry AMD (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025). In vitro assays using human iPSC-derived RPE cells will offer a rigorous platform to measure these effects, including assessments of lysosomal marker expression, autophagy flux (as evidenced by LC3-II conversion), and quantification of lipofuscin reduction (Falcão et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Additionally, the selective reactivation of lysosomal degradation pathways through TFEB translocation is expected to help “reset” the metabolic and catabolic balance in aged RPE cells, thereby contributing to cellular rejuvenation and neuroprotection in the retinal environment (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

The overall evaluation of MSL-7 as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is highly encouraging, primarily based on its mechanistic precision, preclinical dosing feasibility, and the strong theoretical framework underpinning TFEB activation in cellular clearance. One of the key strengths of MSL-7 lies in its ability to selectively manipulate the calcium–calcineurin–TFEB axis without broadly affecting other kinase-driven pathways such as mTOR. Despite these strengths, several challenges and weaknesses must be acknowledged. First, while the mechanism of action of MSL-7 is well elucidated in non-ocular systems, direct evidence for its efficacy and safety in retinal models is still emerging; specifically, there remains a gap in data demonstrating effective delivery, sustained bioavailability, and long-term safety in ocular tissues (Lim et al., 2018; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Another potential limitation is related to the scalability of the therapeutic effect in the complex environment of the human retina, where multiple pathways contribute to disease progression, and it is conceivable that combination therapies may be required to achieve substantial clinical improvement in dry AMD patients (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, while the calcineurin–TFEB pathway is a promising target, its modulation must be finely balanced to avoid excessive autophagic activation, which in some contexts has been associated with detrimental cellular outcomes or even oncogenesis (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Benedetti, 2020).

In summary, the evidence supporting MSL-7 as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD is compelling based on its mechanistic action that directly addresses the pathological accumulation of toxic cellular debris in RPE cells. The ability of MSL-7 to selectively induce TFEB activation via a calcium–calcineurin-mediated pathway distinguishes it from less specific autophagy enhancers and offers the dual benefit of enhanced lysosomal capacity along with improved autophagic flux (Lim et al., 2018). The accumulated literature describing the role of TFEB in neuroprotection and autophagy in the retina, coupled with the favorable pharmacological profile observed in other disease models, provides a strong foundation for the potential translation of MSL-7 into a viable therapeutic option for dry AMD (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Given these considerations, further investigations into MSL-7 should include comprehensive in vitro assays using human iPSC-derived RPE cells to quantify improvements in autophagic flux and the clearance of lipofuscin and A2E aggregates, as well as detailed in vivo studies employing animal models that recapitulate features of dry AMD (Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Parallel efforts should also focus on optimizing drug delivery techniques to the retina to ensure adequate ocular distribution while minimizing systemic exposure. Detailed toxicological assessments will be necessary to determine the long-term safety profile of MSL-7 in retinal tissues, particularly given the chronic nature of AMD treatment regimens (Lim et al., 2018).

In conclusion, while there are clear hurdles that must be overcome before MSL-7 can be considered for clinical trials in dry AMD patients, the mechanistic rationale and preclinical promise of this candidate justify continued research and development. The specificity of MSL-7’s action via the calcium–calcineurin–TFEB pathway provides a targeted approach to enhance the autophagy–lysosomal network in RPE cells, thereby addressing one of the core pathological processes in dry AMD. Continued corroborative data, robust preclinical studies, and strategic formulation approaches will ultimately determine whether MSL-7 can fulfill its promise as a novel therapeutic avenue for this currently unmet clinical need (Lim et al., 2018; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
3,4-Dimethoxychalcone (DMC; Cayman Chemical catalog #CAY32002) is a small synthetic chalcone derivative belonging to the flavonoid family that has emerged in preclinical studies as a potent modulator of autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis. Derived through conventional organic synthetic routes involving aldol condensation reactions between appropriately substituted aromatic aldehydes and acetophenones, DMC exhibits a chalcone scaffold decorated with two methoxy groups that enhance its lipophilicity and potential bioactivity. This compound has been investigated primarily for its ability to stimulate autophagy via transcription factor EB (TFEB) activation, a central regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy that is crucial for cellular clearance mechanisms in postmitotic cells including those in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, chalcones have been explored extensively in the context of longevity, anti‐cancer therapies, and metabolic regulation due to their versatile bioactivity profiles. DMC, in particular, has been reported to induce autophagy and promote lysosomal clearance in various cell types, with evidence emerging from studies in both mammalian cell culture systems and invertebrate models such as Caenorhabditis elegans. Although most of the pre‐clinical investigations using DMC have focused on its beneficial effects in the context of cardiac injury and age‐related neurodegeneration, these studies provide a strong rationale to consider its repurposing for diseases with an autophagy–lysosomal dysfunction component such as dry AMD (Lu et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2024). Furthermore, the literature on alternative TFEB activators—such as trehalose and rapamycin—in RPE cells and AMD models underscore the therapeutic promise of targeting TFEB, even though direct reports of DMC use in AMD models remain limited; instead, the extrapolation of its mechanism from other systems supports its evaluation in RPE-specific assays (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular underpinnings of DMC’s activity center on its capacity to induce TFEB dephosphorylation and promote its nuclear translocation in a manner that appears to bypass the canonical mTORC1 inhibitory pathway. Under homeostatic conditions, TFEB is phosphorylated by mTORC1, which sequesters it in the cytoplasm and limits its transcriptional regulation of genes involved in lysosomal and autophagy pathways. In stress situations, however, TFEB can undergo dephosphorylation—commonly mediated by the phosphatase calcineurin—allowing it to translocate into the nucleus, bind to coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) elements, and upregulate a broad array of lysosomal hydrolases, membrane proteins, and autophagy-related genes (Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2024). DMC is hypothesized to engage this calcineurin–TFEB axis directly, thereby inducing TFEB dephosphorylation without necessitating upstream mTOR inhibition. This mechanism is particularly advantageous given that it avoids the systemic immunosuppressive effects observed with rapamycin-like compounds that target mTOR directly (Gupta et al., 2023; Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025). Importantly, in primary neuronal and epithelial models, treatment with DMC has been reported to increase lysosome number, enhance cathepsin activity, and stimulate autophagic flux, all indicative of robust TFEB activation (Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025). On a biochemical level, the compound appears to trigger a signaling cascade that culminates in the dephosphorylation of key regulatory residues on TFEB, thereby relieving its cytoplasmic retention. Once in the nucleus, TFEB binds to CLEAR network promoters, simultaneously inducing genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis (e.g., LAMP1, Cathepsin D) as well as components of the autophagic machinery, which collectively enhance the cell’s capacity to clear damaged organelles and protein aggregates (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). In the context of dry AMD, the RPE is burdened with the accumulation of photo-oxidized bisretinoids such as A2E and lipofuscin granules, which disrupt normal cellular function and eventually lead to cell death. The evaluation of 3,4-Dimethoxychalcone (DMC) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD presents several compelling strengths alongside certain challenges that must be critically addressed through further research. Among the primary strengths is DMC’s ability to modulate the TFEB pathway in a manner that is claimed to be independent of mTOR inhibition. From a biochemical standpoint, the targeted activation of the calcineurin–TFEB axis by DMC aligns well with current therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring cellular homeostasis in degenerative diseases. By promoting nuclear translocation of TFEB without broadly inhibiting mTOR, DMC could specifically upregulate genes involved not only in lysosomal biogenesis but also in general autophagic processing, thereby addressing both the accumulation of toxic aggregates (such as A2E and lipofuscin granules) and the compromised cellular clearance pathways in the RPE (Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2025). Overall, the repurposing of 3,4-Dimethoxychalcone as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is supported by a solid rationale predicated on its capacity to activate TFEB and enhance autophagic and lysosomal processes in a manner that is potentially independent of mTOR inhibition. Historically, MK-2206 has been the subject of a wide range of preclinical and clinical investigations in the field of oncology. III. Mechanism of Action  
The molecular mechanism of MK-2206 centers on its ability to bind allosterically to AKT isoforms, including AKT1 and AKT2, and induce conformational changes that inhibit the enzyme’s catalytic function. This binding event results in a dose-dependent reduction in the phosphorylation of AKT targets, thereby curtailing the downstream signaling that is critical for cell survival and proliferation (Rehan et al., 2014; Sangai et al., 2012). Recent literature indicates that hyperactivation of AKT2 in RPE cells leads to phosphorylation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of the Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) network (Buniello et al., 2025). Phosphorylated TFEB is sequestered in the cytosol, thereby preventing its nuclear translocation and the induction of genes required for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Under conditions of chronic oxidative stress and extracellular deposit accumulation—hallmarks of dry AMD—impaired TFEB function leads to lysosomal insufficiency, accumulation of toxic waste such as lipofuscin and A2E, and ultimately RPE dysfunction. MK-2206, by inhibiting hyperactive AKT2, is hypothesized to relieve the phosphorylation blockade on TFEB. This would allow TFEB to translocate to the nucleus, activate the expression of the CLEAR network, and restore lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux in RPE cells (Buniello et al., 2025).

Numerous computational and molecular docking studies have further characterized the interaction between MK-2206 and its targets. These studies have pinpointed the key residues within the AKT kinase domain that interact with MK-2206, thereby delineating a molecular basis for the observed decrease in p-AKT levels upon treatment (Rehan et al., 2014; Pal et al., 2010). The specificity of MK-2206 for AKT isoforms is crucial given that complete ablation of all AKT signaling could be deleterious; the goal is instead to selectively dampen the hyperactive AKT2 signaling that is deleterious in RPE cells while avoiding disruption of essential survival pathways in other tissues (Song et al., 2019; Buniello et al., 2025).

In the proposed translational paradigm for dry AMD, MK-2206 is expected to exert a beneficial effect on RPE cell physiology by reversing the lysosomal and autophagic defects that underpin the disease pathology. In vitro assays using induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)–derived RPE cells—cells that recapitulate many aspects of native RPE function—have shown that aberrant AKT2 activity correlates with decreased CLEAR network expression, accumulation of extracellular waste deposition, and compromised mitochondrial function (Buniello et al., 2025). By reducing AKT2-mediated phosphorylation of TFEB, the compound is expected to facilitate TFEB nuclear translocation, thereby restoring transcriptional activation of lysosomal and autophagy genes. The net effect of this intervention would include enhanced lysosomal biogenesis, improved autophagic flux, and accelerated clearance of deleterious lipofuscin aggregates and A2E deposits—a key pathological substrate in dry AMD.

In such models, MK-2206 administration is expected to result in measurable improvements in retinal structure and function, as assessed by techniques like electroretinography (ERG), optical coherence tomography (OCT), and histological analysis of the RPE. The translational attractiveness of MK-2206 is augmented by its well-documented pharmacokinetic safety profile from oncology trials, which provides confidence that repurposing the drug for ocular indications will have a decreased barrier to clinical testing (Coleman et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008).

V. Overall Evaluation  
When considering MK-2206 as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the comprehensive literature review.

Strengths:  
One of the principal advantages of MK-2206 lies in its well-characterized profile in oncology. The robust clinical and preclinical data demonstrate its efficacy in reducing p-AKT levels and inhibiting downstream signaling pathways that contribute to pathological cell proliferation and survival (Coleman et al., 2021; Rehan et al., 2014). This same mechanism of action is directly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, where hyperactive AKT2 disrupts the normal function of TFEB and the CLEAR network, leading to lysosomal dysfunction (Buniello et al., 2025). The fact that MK-2206 is orally bioavailable and has undergone extensive evaluation in phase I and II clinical studies provides a clear translational pathway, as pharmacokinetics, dosing regimens, and safety profiles are already established. This reduces the time and cost associated with early drug development phases, a considerable advantage when repurposing a drug for a new indication. In addition, the specificity of an allosteric inhibitor like MK-2206 offers a mechanism to modulate AKT activity in a context-dependent manner that is less likely to completely ablate signaling and cause systemic toxicity, which is particularly important in a chronic condition such as dry AMD (Sangai et al., 2012). Moreover, the hypothesis that MK-2206 will restore TFEB nuclear translocation provides a mechanistically coherent explanation for how targeting AKT2 can lead to improved lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy in RPE cells—a critical unmet need in dry AMD. This therapeutic intervention targets the core defect in lysosomal/autophagy dysfunction, which is supported by contemporary genetic studies linking AKT2 hyperactivation to accumulation of drusen-associated materials and cellular stress in the RPE (Buniello et al., 2025).

Despite these promising attributes, several potential challenges must be considered in repurposing MK-2206 for dry AMD. First, while extensive oncology data exist, the therapeutic context of dry AMD poses unique challenges related to the ocular environment. The pharmacokinetic behavior of MK-2206 in retinal tissues and its ability to effectively penetrate the blood-retina barrier remain largely uncharacterized. The rationale for targeting the AKT2/TFEB axis in dry AMD is rooted in a deeper understanding of the molecular pathology of the disease. In normal RPE cells, TFEB plays a central role in orchestrating the expression of lysosomal genes and maintaining autophagic flux—a process essential for clearing the daily photoreceptor outer segment shedding and other intracellular waste products. In dry AMD, chronic oxidative stress, compounded by genetic predispositions such as the CFH Y402H variant, results in hyperactivation of AKT2. This hyperactivation leads to aberrant phosphorylation of TFEB, effectively sequestering it in the cytosol and thereby impairing the transcriptional activation of the CLEAR network (Buniello et al., 2025). Such dysregulation results in a cascade of pathological events, including impaired lysosomal function, accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, and ultimately RPE cell degeneration.

MK-2206 is uniquely positioned to counteract this process because its primary mode of action is to inhibit the hyperactive kinase activity of the AKT isoforms, including AKT2, thereby reducing the inhibitory phosphorylation on TFEB. An effective restoration of TFEB nuclear translocation would, in theory, reinitiate the transcription of genes required for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. This molecular intervention has the potential to not only clear accumulated waste products but also to restore mitochondrial function in the RPE—an effect observed in preclinical studies involving other modulators of the AKT2 pathway in genetically modified mouse models and iPSC-derived RPE cells (Buniello et al., 2025).

Molecular docking studies have pinpointed the specific interactions between MK-2206 and the ATP-noncompetitive binding site of AKT, describing how its interaction with critical residues reduces the phosphorylation of downstream targets (Rehan et al., 2014). Such studies provide not only confirmatory evidence for the mechanism of action but also suggest that further optimization or modification of the inhibitor could potentially enhance its selectivity for AKT2 versus other isoforms if needed—an area that would be particularly beneficial for minimizing side effects in the sensitive retinal environment.

Preclinical efforts utilizing iPSC-derived RPE models are particularly informative because they closely mimic the cellular architecture and function of native RPE cells. In these models, pharmacological inhibition of AKT2 using MK-2206 is expected to reverse the phenotype associated with lysosomal dysfunction—namely, the accumulation of intracellular debris, reduced autophagic flux, and compromised mitochondrial activity. In studies that have investigated lysosomal clearance in the context of AMD, an intervention that restores TFEB nuclear localization has been associated with improvements in cell viability and an enhanced capacity to manage oxidative stress (Buniello et al., 2025). The translational pathway for MK-2206 can leverage the extensive clinical data accrued in oncology. Phase I clinical trials in cancer patients have established a dosing regimen and safety profile that, while optimized for tumor suppression, may need to be re-evaluated in the context of ocular drug delivery. The repurposing strategy could involve localized drug delivery systems, such as intravitreal injections or sustained-release ocular implants, to achieve effective drug concentrations in the retina while minimizing systemic exposure and potential adverse effects. One critical parameter that remains to be fully addressed in the context of dry AMD is the selectivity of MK-2206 for AKT2. While many studies have characterized MK-2206 as a pan-AKT inhibitor, preclinical data suggest that its inhibition kinetics may favor certain isoforms under specific conditions (Sangai et al., 2012; Song et al., 2019). The hypothesis posits that selective inhibition of hyperactive AKT2 in the RPE is sufficient to restore TFEB function without completely abolishing all AKT signaling. This nuanced approach is essential because basal AKT activity is required for normal cell survival and metabolism. Future studies should therefore include detailed isoform-specific assays to ensure that the dosing of MK-2206 can be calibrated to achieve the desired reduction in AKT2 activity while preserving the necessary cellular functions mediated by other isoforms.

In addition to these mechanistic considerations, the broader context of dry AMD as a multifactorial disease cannot be overlooked. Dry AMD involves not only lysosomal dysfunction but also chronic inflammation, alterations in extracellular matrix remodeling, and changes in immune cell behavior in the retina. Therefore, while restoring lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic clearance via AKT2 inhibition is a compelling therapeutic strategy, it is likely to need integration with a broader treatment plan that addresses these additional pathogenic components. Combination therapy—where MK-2206 is used together with agents targeting oxidative stress or anti-inflammatory compounds—might yield synergistic benefits and should be a focus of subsequent preclinical investigation.

VII. Conclusion  
In summary, the repurposing of MK-2206 for dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a strong mechanistic rationale and an extensive body of preclinical and clinical evidence from oncology. Its well-validated mechanism as an allosteric pan-AKT inhibitor, combined with emerging data implicating hyperactive AKT2 in the lysosomal dysfunction observed in RPE cells, positions MK-2206 as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025). The expected benefits are manifold: by inhibiting AKT2, MK-2206 is anticipated to relieve the inhibitory phosphorylation of TFEB, enabling its nuclear translocation, which in turn should activate the CLEAR gene network responsible for maintaining lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux. These molecular events are expected to facilitate the clearance of toxic deposits such as lipofuscin and A2E, ultimately protecting the RPE from oxidative stress and drusen-associated damage.

The strengths of MK-2206 include its established clinical safety, oral bioavailability, and detailed pharmacodynamic profile obtained from oncology studies, which together streamline its potential repurposing process. However, several challenges remain, including the need to validate its ocular pharmacokinetics, ensure isoform selectivity in the complex retinal environment, and optimize dosing regimens to prevent potential adverse effects associated with global AKT inhibition. Moreover, long-term safety and efficacy studies in appropriate preclinical models of dry AMD are essential to bridge the gap between preclinical promise and clinical application.

Overall, MK-2206 represents an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on a robust molecular hypothesis, favorable pharmacological properties, and supportive preclinical data suggesting that modulation of the AKT2/TFEB axis can reverse key pathological features of the disease. Continued investigation, including targeted in vitro studies using iPSC-derived RPE cells and relevant animal models, is warranted to further define the therapeutic window and to establish whether the promising benefits observed in preclinical settings translate into meaningful clinical outcomes in patients with dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Coleman et al., 2021; Rehan et al., 2014).

The combination of prior clinical validation in oncology, mechanistic clarity regarding TFEB-mediated lysosomal biogenesis, and the emerging role of AKT2 in the pathogenesis of dry AMD makes MK-2206 a promising candidate in the evolving landscape of AMD therapy. The molecular mechanism of MK-2206 centers on its ability to bind allosterically to AKT isoforms, including AKT1 and AKT2, and induce conformational changes that inhibit the enzyme’s catalytic function. This binding event results in a dose-dependent reduction in the phosphorylation of AKT targets, thereby curtailing the downstream signaling that is critical for cell survival and proliferation (Rehan et al., 2014; Sangai et al., 2012). Recent literature indicates that hyperactivation of AKT2 in RPE cells leads to phosphorylation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of the Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) network (Buniello et al., 2025). Under conditions of chronic oxidative stress and extracellular deposit accumulation—hallmarks of dry AMD—impaired TFEB function leads to lysosomal insufficiency, accumulation of toxic waste such as lipofuscin and A2E, and ultimately RPE dysfunction. MK-2206, by inhibiting hyperactive AKT2, is hypothesized to relieve the phosphorylation blockade on TFEB. This would allow TFEB to translocate to the nucleus, activate the expression of the CLEAR network, and restore lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux in RPE cells (Buniello et al., 2025).

Numerous computational and molecular docking studies have further characterized the interaction between MK-2206 and its targets. These studies have pinpointed the key residues within the AKT kinase domain that interact with MK-2206, thereby delineating a molecular basis for the observed decrease in p-AKT levels upon treatment (Rehan et al., 2014; Pal et al., 2010). The specificity of MK-2206 for AKT isoforms is crucial given that complete ablation of all AKT signaling could be deleterious; the goal is instead to selectively dampen the hyperactive AKT2 signaling that is deleterious in RPE cells while avoiding disruption of essential survival pathways in other tissues (Song et al., 2019; Buniello et al., 2025).

When considering MK-2206 as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the comprehensive literature review.

One of the principal advantages of MK-2206 lies in its well-characterized profile in oncology. The robust clinical and preclinical data demonstrate its efficacy in reducing p-AKT levels and inhibiting downstream signaling pathways that contribute to pathological cell proliferation and survival (Coleman et al., 2021; Rehan et al., 2014). In normal RPE cells, TFEB plays a central role in orchestrating the expression of lysosomal genes and maintaining autophagic flux—a process essential for clearing the daily photoreceptor outer segment shedding and other intracellular waste products. In dry AMD, chronic oxidative stress, compounded by genetic predispositions such as the CFH Y402H variant, results in hyperactivation of AKT2. This hyperactivation leads to aberrant phosphorylation of TFEB, effectively sequestering it in the cytosol and thereby impairing the transcriptional activation of the CLEAR network (Buniello et al., 2025). Such dysregulation results in a cascade of pathological events, including impaired lysosomal function, accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, and ultimately RPE cell degeneration.

MK-2206 is uniquely positioned to counteract this process because its primary mode of action is to inhibit the hyperactive kinase activity of the AKT isoforms, including AKT2, thereby reducing the inhibitory phosphorylation on TFEB. In summary, the repurposing of MK-2206 for dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a strong mechanistic rationale and an extensive body of preclinical and clinical evidence from oncology. In the context of dry AMD, the RPE is burdened with the accumulation of photo-oxidized bisretinoids such as A2E and lipofuscin granules, which disrupt normal cellular function and eventually lead to cell death. The expected pharmacological effect of DMC in relevant assays centers on its capacity to induce TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE cells, consequently upregulating genes that drive lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic clearance. By enhancing the lysosomal degradation machinery, DMC would ideally promote the removal of toxic aggregates associated with oxidative stress and cellular aging, thus preserving RPE cell viability (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). In practical terms, when applied to human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells loaded with A2E, DMC is anticipated to reduce intracellular levels of this toxic byproduct along with the associated lipofuscin burden, thereby mitigating cellular stress and preventing cell death. Thus, in preclinical assays and future in vivo dry AMD models, DMC should manifest as a compound that not only clears deleterious aggregates but also restores overall lysosomal function and cellular homeostasis without the deleterious side effects often associated with mTOR inhibitors (Falcão et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
The evaluation of 3,4-Dimethoxychalcone (DMC) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD presents several compelling strengths alongside certain challenges that must be critically addressed through further research. Among the primary strengths is DMC’s ability to modulate the TFEB pathway in a manner that is claimed to be independent of mTOR inhibition. This mTOR-independent mechanism offers a significant advantage over traditional mTOR inhibitors such as rapamycin, as it theoretically minimizes the risk of systemic immunosuppression and other mTOR-related side effects while still harnessing the potent autophagy-enhancing and lysosome-boosting effects mediated by TFEB (Gupta et al., 2023; Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025). The compound’s demonstrated capacity to increase lysosomal number, stimulate cathepsin activity, and elevate autophagic flux in other cell types further supports its viability as a candidate for clearing chronic intracellular accumulations characteristic of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024).

From a biochemical standpoint, the targeted activation of the calcineurin–TFEB axis by DMC aligns well with current therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring cellular homeostasis in degenerative diseases. By promoting nuclear translocation of TFEB without broadly inhibiting mTOR, DMC could specifically upregulate genes involved not only in lysosomal biogenesis but also in general autophagic processing, thereby addressing both the accumulation of toxic aggregates (such as A2E and lipofuscin granules) and the compromised cellular clearance pathways in the RPE (Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2025). Moreover, the potential engagement of downstream protective pathways—possibly including cross-talk with the NRF2-mediated antioxidative response—accentuates DMC’s promise as a dual-action compound that simultaneously mitigates oxidative stress and improves proteostasis in retinal cells (Falcão et al., 2025).

However, notable weaknesses and uncertainties remain that merit cautious consideration. First, although DMC has been shown in various experimental models to enhance autophagic and lysosomal functions, direct evidence supporting its efficacy specifically in RPE cells or in animal models of dry AMD is currently limited. Most reports detailing its mechanism originate from studies in cardiac and neuronal contexts, leaving a gap in replication and validation within ocular tissues. This translational gap necessitates rigorous preclinical testing using human iPSC-derived RPE cells and established dry AMD animal models to confirm that the TFEB activation observed in other systems translates effectively to the RPE environment (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Another challenge lies in the mechanistic ambiguity surrounding whether DMC acts entirely in an mTOR-independent fashion. Furthermore, while the proposed benefits of enhanced autophagic flux and lysosomal biogenesis are clear, the potential for off-target effects, long-term toxicity, and issues related to drug delivery in the ocular environment must be thoroughly evaluated. Ocular pharmacokinetics can differ markedly from systemic profiles, and the challenges associated with ensuring adequate retinal bioavailability—particularly in the context of the blood–retina barrier—should not be underestimated. An additional consideration is the heterogeneity present among dry AMD patients. The potential for DMC to rescue autophagy-related gene expression and lysosomal function, as suggested by similar findings with TFEB activators in other models, provides a strong impetus for such studies, but careful experimental design will be paramount (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Overall, the repurposing of 3,4-Dimethoxychalcone as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is supported by a solid rationale predicated on its capacity to activate TFEB and enhance autophagic and lysosomal processes in a manner that is potentially independent of mTOR inhibition. Its chemical properties, ease of synthesis, and preliminary evidence from related experimental models collectively argue in favor of its evaluation in RPE-specific assays and animal models of dry AMD. At the same time, key challenges—including the need for clear demonstration of its mTOR-independent mechanism in ocular tissues, comprehensive toxicity profiling, and optimization of drug delivery strategies—must be addressed in subsequent preclinical studies. Given the robust body of literature supporting the critical role of TFEB in maintaining RPE health and mitigating lipofuscin accumulation, DMC stands out as a promising candidate that could offer a novel approach to the treatment of dry AMD, provided that future research confirms its efficacy and safety in the retinal context (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024; Gupta et al., 2023).

In conclusion, the current comprehensive literature review suggests that 3,4-Dimethoxychalcone exhibits significant potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Its unique mechanism of inducing TFEB dephosphorylation and promoting lysosomal biogenesis—thereby enhancing autophagic clearance of photo-oxidized bisretinoids and lipofuscin granules—addresses a fundamental pathogenic process in RPE degeneration. While the preclinical evidence on DMC from non-ocular models is compelling, rigorous validation in RPE-specific systems is essential to definitively establish its role in modulating autophagy and improving retinal cell survival. The strengths of DMC in terms of mechanistic specificity, favorable pharmacological properties, and avoidance of mTOR-related side effects make it a strong candidate for further development, while the challenges associated with direct translation to ocular models underscore the need for carefully designed preclinical studies. As such, the proposed direction for our drug development effort should focus on detailed in vitro assays using human iPSC-derived RPE cells, followed by in vivo evaluation in dry AMD animal models, to fully delineate the therapeutic potential and safety profile of DMC for clinical application in dry AMD (Gupta et al., 2023; Carmona-Gutierrez et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2019).

In addition to the common hydroxamate zinc-binding motif, structural modifications such as the incorporation of a rigid, selectively tuned carbazole cap have contributed to Tubastatin A’s high selectivity for HDAC6 over other isoforms (Butler et al., 2010; Shen & Kozikowski, 2020a). As a member of a growing portfolio of HDAC6 inhibitors that originated from oncology and neurodegenerative research, Tubastatin A offers a well-documented chemical scaffold that has been optimized for both potency—with an IC₅₀ of approximately 15 nM—and favorable pharmacological properties including significant selectivity and in vivo tolerability (Wang, Wan, & Liu, 2018; Butler et al., 2010). Its synthetic origin and evolution from earlier molecules exemplify current trends in epigenetic drug discovery, where the focus is on generating compounds with high specificity toward individual HDAC family members to mitigate off-target effects while maintaining anticancer or neuroprotective efficacy (Batchu, Brijmohan, & Advani, 2016; Cosenza & Pozzi, 2018).

In cancer research, Tubastatin A and its diarylamine- and hydroxamate-based analogs have been leveraged for their ability to selectively inhibit HDAC6-mediated deacetylation, thereby restoring acetylation of α-tubulin and counteracting aberrant cellular processes that are characteristic of malignant transformation. For instance, studies in multiple myeloma models have shown that selective inhibition of HDAC6 can create a therapeutic window that minimizes the collateral effects frequently observed with broad-spectrum HDAC inhibitors (Simões-Pires, Bertrand, & Cuendet, 2017). Parallel to its oncology applications, Tubastatin A has been assessed in a number of neuroprotective paradigms, where its action in increasing tubulin acetylation has been linked to the restoration of axonal transport mechanisms, mitochondrial dynamics, and overall neuronal integrity (Wang, Wan, & Liu, 2018; Butler et al., 2010). In rodent models of tauopathy and other neurodegenerative conditions, inhibition of HDAC6 with Tubastatin A has resulted in improvements in behavioral outcomes and the reduction of toxic protein aggregates, thereby lending credence to its molecular mechanism of action and efficacy in improving cellular autophagy (Kalin & Bergman, 2013; Selenica et al., 2014). The principal substrate of HDAC6 is α-tubulin, a major component of the microtubule network, whose acetylation status is critical for maintaining microtubule stability and facilitating intracellular transport events (Wang, Wan, & Liu, 2018; Butler et al., 2010). By binding to the active site of HDAC6 through its hydroxamate zinc-binding group, Tubastatin A chelates the catalytic zinc ion and thereby blocks the deacetylation reaction, leading to an accumulation of acetylated α-tubulin (Butler et al., 2010; Shen & Kozikowski, 2020a). Developed through iterative medicinal chemistry optimization processes that sought to overcome resistance to first‐generation inhibitors such as imatinib, nilotinib is structurally designed to selectively bind the ATP-binding pocket of the c-Abl kinase, thereby inhibiting its catalytic activity (Karim et al., 2020). As a representative member of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), nilotinib falls into the class of targeted anticancer agents that have been widely used in oncology, with extensive preclinical and clinical experience in modulating aberrant kinase signaling pathways. The synthetic origins of nilotinib involve derivatization of earlier BCR–ABL inhibitors to improve potency and specificity, and its development has been a model for the design of targeted agents in diseases driven by kinase dysregulation (Karim et al., 2020). While its initial application has been in CML, its potent inhibition of c-Abl has attracted attention for repurposing in other conditions where this kinase plays a pathological role, including neurodegeneration and, as hypothesized here, dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Karim et al., 2020; Fowler et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Nilotinib has a well-documented clinical history as an FDA-approved therapeutic for CML, where its efficacy and safety profile have been established across numerous clinical trials and long-term follow-up studies. Over the past decade, repurposing efforts have extended into neurodegenerative diseases based on its ability to cross the blood–brain barrier (albeit at modest concentrations) and modulate pathogenic protein aggregation via autophagy enhancement. Preclinical studies in models of α-synucleinopathy, Parkinson’s disease, and Alzheimer’s disease have demonstrated that nilotinib can reduce toxic protein burden, improve autophagic clearance, and rescue neuronal survival by inhibiting c-Abl mediated pathways (Karim et al., 2020). Despite these promising findings in neurological contexts, a systematic search of clinical trial databases reveals that nilotinib has not yet been directly investigated in dry AMD or related retinal degenerative conditions (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). This lack of prior clinical evaluation in the retinal domain represents both a gap in the evidence base and an opportunity for further translational research, building on the extensive safety and pharmacokinetic data already available from its oncological and neurodegenerative applications (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central mechanism of nilotinib is its inhibition of the aberrantly activated c-Abl tyrosine kinase. Under normal conditions, c-Abl regulates various cellular processes, including cell-cycle control, DNA repair, and stress responses. However, in pathological settings such as CML and certain neurodegenerative diseases, c-Abl becomes hyperactivated, leading to detrimental downstream effects including the activation of the tumor suppressor p53 via phosphorylation (Karim et al., 2020). In neurodegenerative models, c-Abl activation has been shown to interfere with autophagy, a critical intracellular degradation process, by upregulating p53 and inhibiting key autophagy initiators such as ULK1 and Beclin1 (Karim et al., 2020). Mechanistic studies in α-synucleinopathy models have demonstrated that nilotinib’s inhibition of c-Abl reduces the phosphorylation of p53 and decreases downstream mTORC1 signaling, thereby releasing autophagic blockades (Karim et al., 2020). Specifically, nilotinib treatment has been shown to enhance autophagic flux through increased conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II and reduced accumulation of the autophagy adaptor p62, indicating improved autophagosome formation and lysosomal clearance (Karim et al., 2020). Moreover, by inhibiting c-Abl, nilotinib alleviates the phosphorylation of ULK1 and enables its activation in an AMPK-dependent manner, which is critical for the initiation of autophagy; there is also emerging evidence that this inhibition may drive the formation or activation of the Beclin1 complex, further promoting autophagosome nucleation (Karim et al., 2020). Thus, nilotinib exerts a dual effect: it directly impedes the kinase activity of c-Abl while indirectly reactivating autophagic pathways that are otherwise suppressed by c-Abl’s pathological signaling via p53 and mTOR (Karim et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesized role of c-Abl in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, it is anticipated that nilotinib will have several beneficial effects in the context of dry AMD. In RPE cells, chronic oxidative stress and drusen-associated stressors are known to activate c-Abl, leading to the phosphorylation and inhibition of key autophagy regulators such as ULK1 and Beclin1. This interruption of autophagic flux is believed to contribute to lipofuscin accumulation, particularly of A2E, a toxic by-product implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Kim, Hwang, & Kwon, 2020; Karim et al., 2020). By inhibiting c-Abl, nilotinib should theoretically reverse this block, restore ULK1/Beclin1 activity, and re-establish effective autophagic clearance. In in vitro RPE cell assays that employ stresses such as A2E challenge and oxidative insults, nilotinib is expected to decrease the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, increase markers of autophagic flux such as LC3-II, and reduce p62 levels, thereby indicating enhanced lysosomal degradation (Kim, Hwang, & Kwon, 2020; Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024). With improved autophagic processing, the cellular homeostasis within RPE cells should be restored, thereby preventing the degenerative changes that contribute to drusen formation and the overall progression of dry AMD. Furthermore, animal studies in neurodegenerative models have shown that nilotinib can lead to delayed onset of clinical symptoms and improved cell survival, lending support to the potential translational value of these mechanisms in the retinal environment (Karim et al., 2020). It is important to note that while supportive mechanistic evidence exists from neurodegeneration research, direct experimental validation of nilotinib’s impact on RPE autophagy and lipofuscin clearance in dry AMD-specific models remains to be performed (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
Nilotinib represents a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration due to its well-characterized pharmacological profile, established safety through its use in CML, and promising mechanistic insights from neurodegeneration studies. One of the primary strengths of this candidate is its clear molecular mechanism: by inhibiting c-Abl, nilotinib has the potential to reverse the autophagy blockade mediated by pathological p53 activation and mTOR signaling, a mechanism that is plausibly relevant to the pathology observed in RPE cells under oxidative and drusen stress (Karim et al., 2020). The existing literature strongly supports the notion that c-Abl plays a pivotal role in autophagy regulation, with multiple studies demonstrating that its inhibition leads to enhanced autophagic clearance of toxic protein aggregates in neuronal models (Karim et al., 2020; Kim, Hwang, & Kwon, 2020). This mechanistic similarity is particularly encouraging given that autophagic dysfunction and accumulation of cellular debris such as lipofuscin (and its A2E component) are central to the progression of dry AMD (Kim, Hwang, & Kwon, 2020; Karim et al., 2020).

Another strength is the translational potential based on nilotinib’s pharmacokinetic profile. Despite challenges often associated with drug delivery to the central nervous system and ocular tissues, nilotinib has demonstrated the ability to cross the blood–brain barrier at pharmacologically relevant doses, suggesting that similar (albeit low-dose) penetration of the blood–retina barrier might be achievable. This is supported by the documented systemic administration protocols in preclinical neurodegeneration models where nilotinib exhibited biological activity in brain tissues (Karim et al., 2020), and by extension, such dosing strategies may be adapted for ocular tissues. The fact that nilotinib is already FDA-approved means that its safety profile, dosing parameters, and potential side effects are well understood, which significantly reduces the risk and accelerates the timeline for repurposing in a new indication (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024).

However, there are several weaknesses and challenges that must be acknowledged. First, despite the promising mechanistic data in neurodegenerative models, direct evidence for nilotinib’s efficacy in RPE cells and in models of dry AMD is currently lacking. A systematic search of clinical trial databases has revealed no registered trials for nilotinib in the context of AMD, which suggests that while preclinical data in other systems is robust, the translational leap to retinal applications remains uncharted (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Moreover, the molecular environment in the retina, particularly within the RPE, may differ in significant ways from neuronal tissues; factors such as differential expression patterns of autophagy regulators, variations in stress response signaling, and the unique barrier properties of the retina may influence nilotinib’s ultimate efficacy (Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024; Kim, Hwang, & Kwon, 2020).

Another potential concern is the specificity of nilotinib’s activity in the ocular environment. While its primary mechanism is through c-Abl inhibition, nilotinib has been documented to interact with other kinases (such as DDR1/DDR2) at low nanomolar concentrations (Fowler et al., 2019), which could lead to off-target effects that may be undesirable in the delicate architecture of the retina. These off-target interactions could potentially disrupt normal cellular processes within the retina, potentially exacerbating rather than ameliorating retinal degeneration if not carefully controlled (Fowler et al., 2019; Hussain et al., 2019). Additionally, while nilotinib’s safety profile has been demonstrated in systemic oncology settings, the safety and tolerability of chronic nilotinib administration directly affecting ocular tissues have yet to be thoroughly evaluated. Intraocular injections or other targeted delivery methods might be required to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina, and these routes carry their own risks of complications, including infection and retinal detachment (Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024).

In summary, nilotinib offers a conceptually appealing avenue for the treatment of dry AMD by targeting a clear molecular driver—c-Abl mediated autophagy dysfunction—that is implicated in the accumulation of toxic aggregates in RPE cells. The extensive preclinical data from neurodegenerative models provides a strong foundation that supports the hypothesis that nilotinib can restore autophagic flux by reactivating ULK1/Beclin1 function and reducing p53-mediated inhibition (Karim et al., 2020). The fact that nilotinib is already approved for human use and has well-characterized pharmacokinetics and safety data further enhances its attractiveness for repurposing. Nonetheless, significant hurdles remain, most notably the absence of direct evidence in retinal models, potential differences in drug permeability and target engagement in RPE cells, and the risk of off-target effects in ocular tissues. These challenges underscore the need for rigorous preclinical validation in RPE culture systems (e.g., using A2E challenge assays) and well-designed dry AMD animal models before advancing to clinical trials (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Santos, Ambrósio, & Léger, 2024).

Overall, given its mechanistic rationale, previous efficacy in related neurodegenerative contexts, and favorable safety profile in oncology, nilotinib stands out as a promising candidate for further exploration as a treatment for dry AMD. Its repurposing offers a high translational value with the potential to address a major unmet medical need, provided that future studies can confirm its ability to cross the blood–retina barrier, restore autophagic processing in RPE cells, and ultimately prevent RPE degeneration without incurring significant ocular toxicity (Fowler et al., 2019; Karim et al., 2020). Continued interdisciplinary research involving detailed biochemical studies, targeted delivery assessments, and in vivo pharmacodynamic evaluations will be critical to fully validate nilotinib’s therapeutic potential in the context of dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
MSL-7 is a potent, synthetic small‐molecule activator of transcription factor EB (TFEB) that was discovered through high‐content screening methodologies and is commercially available (Cayman Chemical catalog #14818). This candidate belongs to a novel class of autophagy enhancers that exploit the calcium–calcineurin signaling pathway rather than the classical mTOR inhibition mechanism to induce nuclear translocation of TFEB (Lim et al., 2018). Unlike many mTOR inhibitors that produce a broader range of kinase and metabolic inhibition with considerable off‐target effects, MSL-7 is designed to selectively elevate cytosolic calcium in target cells, leading to the activation of the phosphatase calcineurin and subsequent dephosphorylation of TFEB (Lim et al., 2018). Subsequently, dephosphorylated TFEB translocates to the nucleus, where it binds to coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) motifs and activates the transcription of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Chen et al., 2021). As a member of the small-molecule TFEB activators, MSL-7 represents a targeted therapeutic approach that has been primarily studied for metabolic disorders and neurodegenerative conditions and now is being considered for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) due to the critical role of lysosomal dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) pathology (Lim et al., 2018; Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of molecules that modulate TFEB activity spans multiple disease areas, including metabolic syndrome, neurodegeneration, and lysosomal storage disorders. MSL-7 itself has been evaluated in preclinical models for metabolic syndrome, showing promising metabolic improvements via its activation of the calcium–calcineurin–TFEB axis (Lim et al., 2018). In these studies, MSL-7 reversed metabolic changes through enhanced autophagic flux and improved lysosomal clearance, setting a precedent for its application in diseases where accumulation of toxic aggregates is central to pathology (Lim et al., 2018). Although MSL-7 has not been directly used for the treatment of dry AMD in clinical studies, considerable evidence from biochemical and cellular studies supports the concept that activation of TFEB can ameliorate age-dependent RPE dysfunction by promoting the clearance of lipofuscin and other toxic aggregates (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025). Prior studies of other TFEB activators—such as trehalose, which has been shown to enhance autophagic clearance in RPE cells—provide a robust rationale for the application of MSL-7 in retinal degenerative models (Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Moreover, the involvement of the autophagy–lysosomal network in maintaining retinal health and its impairment in AMD have been well documented, suggesting that strategies to enhance autophagic clearance via TFEB activation are both mechanistically sound and therapeutically appealing (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism of MSL-7 centers on its ability to modulate intracellular calcium dynamics, which is critical for the activation of the phosphatase calcineurin. Under physiological conditions, TFEB remains phosphorylated and sequestered in the cytoplasm by the action of mTORC1 and possibly other kinases; however, when MSL-7 is applied, it elevates cytosolic calcium levels specifically in RPE cells, thereby leading to the activation of calcineurin via calcium–calmodulin interactions (Lim et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020). Activated calcineurin then dephosphorylates TFEB at key serine residues, resulting in its release from cytoplasmic retention complexes and enabling its translocation to the nucleus (Lim et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020). Once in the nucleus, TFEB binds to CLEAR network promoters, initiating the transcription of a suite of genes that are essential for lysosomal biogenesis, catabolic enzyme production, and enhanced autophagic flux (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Chen et al., 2021). This transcriptional upregulation leads to an increased lysosomal capacity, improved degradation of intracellular aggregates, and enhanced recycling of damaged organelles, which is particularly beneficial in the context of RPE cells that are burdened with the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E—byproducts of photoreceptor outer segment degradation (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). The specificity of MSL-7 for the calcium–calcineurin pathway is a significant advantage, as it circumvents typical mTOR-dependent pathways and thereby minimizes the risk of widespread metabolic disruption, offering a focused therapeutic effect on the autophagy–lysosomal system (Lim et al., 2018). In addition, the robustness of the mechanism is enhanced by the fact that TFEB activation has been shown to be beneficial in a number of models related to protein aggregation and cellular clearance, including neuronal and hepatic systems, thus providing a biochemical blueprint for its potential utility in RPE repair and dry AMD intervention (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Expected Effect:  
When applied to human iPSC-derived RPE models of dry AMD that exhibit lipofuscin accumulation, MSL-7 is hypothesized to restore cellular homeostasis by robustly enhancing autophagic flux and lysosomal biogenesis. The expected cellular effects include an elevated clearance of lipofuscin-like granules and A2E, which are hallmark toxic deposits in RPE cells and are directly implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025). By upregulating CLEAR network genes via the nuclear activity of TFEB, MSL-7 is anticipated to increase the number and functional capacity of lysosomes, thereby accelerating the degradation of damaged cellular components and misfolded proteins that contribute to RPE atrophy (Falcão et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). This enhanced clearance mechanism is particularly relevant given that the accumulation of oxidized biomolecules and damaged organelles in RPE cells is a critical factor that underlies aging-associated retinal degeneration, as evidenced by multiple studies linking TFEB activity to neuroprotection in the retina (Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Moreover, the augmentation of autophagic capacity is expected not only to mitigate the deleterious buildup of cellular waste but also to reduce pro-inflammatory signaling and oxidative stress—a dual mechanism that could slow disease progression and preserve visual acuity in patients with dry AMD (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025). In vitro assays using human iPSC-derived RPE cells will offer a rigorous platform to measure these effects, including assessments of lysosomal marker expression, autophagy flux (as evidenced by LC3-II conversion), and quantification of lipofuscin reduction (Falcão et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). The overall evaluation of MSL-7 as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is highly encouraging, primarily based on its mechanistic precision, preclinical dosing feasibility, and the strong theoretical framework underpinning TFEB activation in cellular clearance. One of the key strengths of MSL-7 lies in its ability to selectively manipulate the calcium–calcineurin–TFEB axis without broadly affecting other kinase-driven pathways such as mTOR. Moreover, the experimental paradigm of using human iPSC-derived RPE models represents a state-of-the-art strategy, enabling direct observation of the drug’s effect on human retinal cells that model the disease pathology, thereby increasing the relevance of preclinical findings to clinical outcomes (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Despite these strengths, several challenges and weaknesses must be acknowledged. First, while the mechanism of action of MSL-7 is well elucidated in non-ocular systems, direct evidence for its efficacy and safety in retinal models is still emerging; specifically, there remains a gap in data demonstrating effective delivery, sustained bioavailability, and long-term safety in ocular tissues (Lim et al., 2018; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Moreover, while the calcineurin–TFEB pathway is a promising target, its modulation must be finely balanced to avoid excessive autophagic activation, which in some contexts has been associated with detrimental cellular outcomes or even oncogenesis (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Benedetti, 2020).

In summary, the evidence supporting MSL-7 as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD is compelling based on its mechanistic action that directly addresses the pathological accumulation of toxic cellular debris in RPE cells. The ability of MSL-7 to selectively induce TFEB activation via a calcium–calcineurin-mediated pathway distinguishes it from less specific autophagy enhancers and offers the dual benefit of enhanced lysosomal capacity along with improved autophagic flux (Lim et al., 2018). The accumulated literature describing the role of TFEB in neuroprotection and autophagy in the retina, coupled with the favorable pharmacological profile observed in other disease models, provides a strong foundation for the potential translation of MSL-7 into a viable therapeutic option for dry AMD (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Given these considerations, further investigations into MSL-7 should include comprehensive in vitro assays using human iPSC-derived RPE cells to quantify improvements in autophagic flux and the clearance of lipofuscin and A2E aggregates, as well as detailed in vivo studies employing animal models that recapitulate features of dry AMD (Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Parallel efforts should also focus on optimizing drug delivery techniques to the retina to ensure adequate ocular distribution while minimizing systemic exposure. Detailed toxicological assessments will be necessary to determine the long-term safety profile of MSL-7 in retinal tissues, particularly given the chronic nature of AMD treatment regimens (Lim et al., 2018).

In conclusion, while there are clear hurdles that must be overcome before MSL-7 can be considered for clinical trials in dry AMD patients, the mechanistic rationale and preclinical promise of this candidate justify continued research and development. The specificity of MSL-7’s action via the calcium–calcineurin–TFEB pathway provides a targeted approach to enhance the autophagy–lysosomal network in RPE cells, thereby addressing one of the core pathological processes in dry AMD. Continued corroborative data, robust preclinical studies, and strategic formulation approaches will ultimately determine whether MSL-7 can fulfill its promise as a novel therapeutic avenue for this currently unmet clinical need (Lim et al., 2018; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate: Tubastatin A is a fully synthetic, selective inhibitor of histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6) that belongs to the hydroxamate-based class of HDAC inhibitors and is also classified among diarylamine-based derivatives. Originally inspired by the structure of tubacin, Tubastatin A was conceived through rational, structure-based drug design employing modern medicinal chemistry approaches that take advantage of the unique dimensions and catalytic zinc‐dependent active site of HDAC6 (Simões-Pires, Bertrand, & Cuendet, 2017; Wang, Wan, & Liu, 2018). Its chemical synthesis is characterized by straightforward methodologies involving less than five linear steps, which not only streamlines the production process but also facilitates the rapid derivation of analog series for further preclinical development (Simões-Pires, Bertrand, & Cuendet, 2017; Batchu, Brijmohan, & Advani, 2016). In addition to the common hydroxamate zinc-binding motif, structural modifications such as the incorporation of a rigid, selectively tuned carbazole cap have contributed to Tubastatin A’s high selectivity for HDAC6 over other isoforms (Butler et al., 2010; Shen & Kozikowski, 2020a). As a member of a growing portfolio of HDAC6 inhibitors that originated from oncology and neurodegenerative research, Tubastatin A offers a well-documented chemical scaffold that has been optimized for both potency—with an IC₅₀ of approximately 15 nM—and favorable pharmacological properties including significant selectivity and in vivo tolerability (Wang, Wan, & Liu, 2018; Butler et al., 2010). Its synthetic origin and evolution from earlier molecules exemplify current trends in epigenetic drug discovery, where the focus is on generating compounds with high specificity toward individual HDAC family members to mitigate off-target effects while maintaining anticancer or neuroprotective efficacy (Batchu, Brijmohan, & Advani, 2016; Cosenza & Pozzi, 2018).

In cancer research, Tubastatin A and its diarylamine- and hydroxamate-based analogs have been leveraged for their ability to selectively inhibit HDAC6-mediated deacetylation, thereby restoring acetylation of α-tubulin and counteracting aberrant cellular processes that are characteristic of malignant transformation. For instance, studies in multiple myeloma models have shown that selective inhibition of HDAC6 can create a therapeutic window that minimizes the collateral effects frequently observed with broad-spectrum HDAC inhibitors (Simões-Pires, Bertrand, & Cuendet, 2017). Thus, from a therapeutic history perspective, Tubastatin A’s well-characterized profile in non-ocular systems and its mechanistic implications on autophagy present a compelling rationale for its evaluation as a candidate for dry AMD, while also noting that direct studies in retinal models remain a gap to be addressed in future investigations (Kalin & Bergman, 2013; Selenica et al., 2014).

Mechanism of Action: At the molecular level, Tubastatin A exerts its pharmacological effects by selectively inhibiting HDAC6, a cytoplasmic enzyme that is uniquely involved in the deacetylation of non-histone proteins. Nevertheless, there remain some concerns and challenges that warrant attention. One of the primary weaknesses lies in the current paucity of direct evidence supporting Tubastatin A’s efficacy in ocular models or its ability to effectively penetrate the blood–retina barrier (Buniello et al., 2025; Kalin & Bergman, 2013). Furthermore, while the mechanistic data from neurodegenerative and oncological studies are compelling, translating these effects to the context of dry AMD will require careful verification in retinal-specific in vitro and in vivo systems. The candidate’s chemical and pharmacological attributes, which have been validated in parts through oncology and neurodegenerative research, align well with the proposed mechanism of action whereby impaired autophagosome–lysosome fusion contributes to RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. While pre-existing data primarily focus on its anti-tumor and neuroprotective roles, the mechanistic similarities shared between neuronal autophagic deficits and RPE deficits under oxidative stress conditions support the hypothesis that Tubastatin A may improve autophagic clearance of lipofuscin and A2E, thereby preserving RPE integrity (Kalin & Bergman, 2013; Buniello et al., 2025; Shen & Kozikowski, 2020a).

Moving forward, it will be critical to design rigorous preclinical studies using iPSC-derived RPE cells and appropriate animal models to evaluate the pharmacokinetics, ocular bioavailability, and long-term safety of Tubastatin A in the retinal setting. On balance, despite the current gaps in direct evidence for ocular applications, the strengths—including its targeted mechanism, robust safety profile in non-ocular systems, and ease of synthesis—position Tubastatin A as an attractive candidate for repurposing. It represents a scientifically sound and strategically promising approach to address the autophagic dysfunction underlying dry AMD, thereby meriting further investigation as part of an innovative therapeutic strategy (Wang, Wan, & Liu, 2018; Butler et al., 2010; Shen & Kozikowski, 2020a; Shen et al., 2020b).
